A1.text:
Court grants ex-Malaysian PM Najib house arrest after $12m royal pardon
Najib transitions to house arrest after his party UMNO raises $12m fine via crowdfunding.
Malaysia’s jailed former Prime Minister Najib Razak is set to transfer from prison to house arrest after his party paid a $12m fine following a royal pardon.
Najib’s lawyer, Farhan Shafee, told reporters on Friday that he has been given the order and will be “delivering that order to the Kajang prison right now”. His house arrest could start on Friday if everything goes to plan, Shafee said.
However, Malaysia’s attorney general announced on Friday that Najib’s transfer had been temporarily suspended. In a statement, reported by Reuters, the chambers of the attorney general said Najib’s current detention status in prison “will be maintained as some legal questions regarding the interpretation of Najib’s conditional royal pardon need clarifying”.
Najib, who denies any wrongdoing, has been held in jail since 2022, following his conviction for corruption and embezzlement of billions of dollars connected to 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB), a state investment fund he cofounded while in power from 2009-2018.
The order comes after Malaysia’s King Sultan Ibrahim agreed in September to pardon Najib, allowing him to serve the rest of his sentence at home.
Najib’s party, the United Malays National Organisation, has reportedly used crowdfunding to cover Najib’s 50 million ringgit ($12m) fine, as his bank accounts have been frozen.
Al Jazeera’s Rob McBride, reporting from Kuala Lumpur, said this decision could cause a political stir in Malaysia.
“This has an awful lot of political spinoff, potentially impacting the political scene here in Malaysia,” he said. “But also there’s a lot of questions being asked about how the current politics have impacted this pardon.”
He said Anwar Ibrahim, the prime minister of Malaysia, has publicly raised concerns about the pardon within his capacity as the “anticorruption figurehead” in the country. But there has been speculation that he may have, behind the scenes, helped the pardon go through due to pressure from Najib’s party.
Investigators say about $4.5bn was stolen from the 1MDB state fund and more than $1bn of it was linked to Najib.
Najib has said he was solely blamed for a highly complicated global fraud scheme and has denied any wrongdoing.
Separately, he was also convicted in a major 1MBD trial in Malaysia, where he was sentenced to 15 years in prison and a $2.5bn fine for money laundering and the abuse of power.
He has appealed the case and his lawyers requested that the jail term and fines be halted, citing poor health and his inability to pay the fine.
A judge rejected his request in September, saying “the gravity of the offence is a more important public interest consideration”. Al Jazeera’s McBride said Najib is due to return to jail to serve out this sentence as soon as his house arrest ends in 2028, but it is unclear at this stage if this will happen.

A103.text:
Leo, who is 71 and underwent lung cancer surgery last month, will visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru through November 17 on one of the most demanding overseas tours taken by a Catholic leader in decades.
The Vatican said this week that the pope had completely healed from his operation and no special precautions were being taken for the tour, on which Leo will travel some 31,000 km (19,300 miles) across 10 cities and give 36 speeches.
The pope, who was born in Chicago but spent decades in Peru and became a Peruvian citizen, considers the tour a "homecoming to places where he spent a long time and to which he feels closely connected," said Vatican spokesperson Matteo Bruni.
Leo told pilgrims at his weekly audience in St. Peter's Square on Wednesday that during the trip he was hoping to "strengthen the faith, renew hope, (and) rekindle the fire of charity".
POPE EXPECTED TO ADDRESS REGIONAL INSTABILITY
The pope, who departed fromRome's Fiumicino airport early on Friday morning, is due to arrive in Uruguay at 4:30 p.m. (1930 GMT). He will stay in the country until Sunday, visiting three cities before continuing on for three days in Argentina and six days in Peru.
Leo, who has forcefully decried the direction of global leadership in recent months, will address the governments in each country in closely watched speeches. He will also lead outdoor Masses at major local sites, visit a prison in Argentina and head to remote Andean communities in Peru by helicopter.
On Sunday, Leo will give an address to Argentine President Javier Milei, a right-wing libertarian seen as a close ally to US President Donald Trump, who lambasted Leo earlier this year after the pope criticized the Iran war.
Bruni said the pope's speeches during the tour would address a range of issues facing the continent, including environmental destruction, arms trafficking and regional political instability.
"The pope brings a message of communion and unity, an invitation to recognise one another ... as members of one same family," he said.
The late Pope Francis, who was Leo's predecessor and from Argentina, visited Peru in 2018 but never returned home. A pope has not visited Argentina or Uruguay since the late 1980s.
Argentine officials have said some 7 million people will attend events with Leo.
VATICAN NOT TAKING ADDITIONAL MEDICAL PRECAUTIONS
Latin America has long been the world's largest Catholic region in absolute numbers, but the Church has been losing ground recently to fast-growing evangelical denominations and has struggled to respond to progressive social attitudes and individualized forms of worship.
Local Catholic leaders hope Leo's visit can reenergize the faith across the region and also help repair the Church's standing after abuse scandals have tarnished its reputation.
Leo will hold several meetings with survivors of sexual abuse by Catholic clergy during the trip, the Vatican has said, without yet providing further details.
The pope was treated in October for lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer. His doctors have said the disease was localized and he would not require any further treatments.
Bruni said Leo had recovered enough that no additional medical measures would be necessary during his trip.
Medical experts told Reuters the decision by Leo's doctors to clear him to fly should indicate the risk of complications from his surgery was low, that his operated lung had fully expanded and any surgical wounds were healing without signs of infection.
They suggested, however, that Leo might need to take rest breaks to deal with the trip's intense itinerary and consider using supplemental oxygen as needed, especially during his high-altitude visits in the Peruvian Andes.
(Reporting by Joshua McElwee; additional reporting by Lucinda Elliott in Montevideo, Cassandra Garrison in Mexico City, and Marco Aquino in Lima; Editing by Alexandra Hudson)

CROWDFUNDING TO SEND NAJIB HOME

In the 1MDB scandal, more than $1 billion allegedly made its way into accounts linked to Najib, who says he has been made the scapegoat for a complex, globe-spanning scheme that siphoned away as much as $4.5 billion in funds, according to US investigators.

Though the next election is not due to take place until early 2028, Anwar has said he could call a snap poll if rifts deepen.
Tony Pua, a former DAP lawmaker who played a key role in drawing attention to the 1MDB scandal, said Najib was "Malaysia's biggest crook" and chided UMNO for raising funds for him.
"Instead of using such a large sum of money to help ordinary Malaysians, they chose to 'free' Malaysia's most corrupt," he said on Facebook.

A11.text:
Israel’s President Herzog to name candidate to form government on Sunday
Announcement comes after majority of Israeli lawmakers endorse Eisenkot over Netanyahu.
Israel’s President Isaac Herzog has said he will name a candidate to form the country’s next government by Sunday, after a majority of lawmakers backed opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Herzog made the announcement on Thursday after holding marathon talks with parties elected to the 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset.
Some 67 lawmakers endorsed Eisenkot, a former military chief, while 46 backed Netanyahu.
In televised remarks at the end of the talks, Herzog said that although the “results of the consultations may appear clear”, there were “mutual vetoes between the blocs and within the blocs themselves” that make it difficult to say who has the best chance of assembling a governing coalition.
He said he would hold “personal talks with some of the party leaders” over the Israeli weekend, which runs Friday-Saturday, and make a pick on Sunday.
Israel’s October 27 election left neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot with a clear path to a parliamentary majority, handing Herzog the difficult task of choosing a candidate in a deeply divided country.
Netanyahu’s Likud won the most seats of any single party with 27 in the 120-seat Knesset, but his wider religious-nationalist coalition garnered only 53 in total.
Eisenkot’s alliance of four Jewish-led parties, which spans the political spectrum from centre-left to right, won 48 seats despite polls that had predicted a close race.
Two parties representing Israel’s Palestinian minority won an unprecedented 19 seats.
Eisenkot, like Netanyahu, has ruled out forming a government with the Arab-led parties. Both of those parties nonetheless recommended him, giving him the support of a comfortable majority of lawmakers.
“We want to do things that we did not do in the past in order to remove this criminal government,” Ahmad Tibi, a senior member of the Joint List, which represents an alliance of Arab parties, told The Associated Press news agency.
Eisenkot’s party, Yashar, said his 67 recommendations were the most any candidate had received since 2015, and urged Herzog to give him the mandate “as soon as possible” so he could form a national emergency government.
Separately, Netanyahu suffered a setback on Thursday when United Torah Judaism, one of the two main ultra-Orthodox parties and a longtime ally, declined to recommend any candidate.
The party broke with Netanyahu over his coalition’s failure to pass legislation exempting ultra-Orthodox men from military service, The Times of Israel reported.
Yariv Oppenheimer, a member of the Democrats, a party in Eisenkot’s alliance, told Al Jazeera that he saw “no reason” Herzog would not choose Eisenkot on Sunday.
He said United Torah Judaism had signalled that its support was available for the right price, meaning that a good enough offer from Eisenkot could give him the numbers he needed.
“It’s very clear that Netanyahu doesn’t have a chance to establish a government at all,” he added.
Once nominated by Herzog, the candidate will have 28 days to try to forge a government, with a possible 14-day extension.
Netanyahu will remain prime minister in a caretaker government until a new coalition is formed, or through another election that must be held if no candidate succeeds.
Netanyahu, at risk of losing power, has seized on an investigation by election officials into possible vote tampering to cast doubt on the results, accusing Arab-led parties of stealing the vote.
Critics accuse Netanyahu and his partners of trying to undermine the results, which he denies.
Israel’s Central Election Committee said on Wednesday that the election’s integrity had not been compromised. The head of the committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, has called on Israel’s elected officials to protect public trust rather than shake it.

A133.text:
Ukraineverhandlungen mit Russland Trump stellt nach Treffen mit Kremlberater Abkommen für »ganz Europa« in Aussicht
US-Präsident Donald Trump hat nach Gesprächen mit Vertretern Russlands ein »sehr großes« Abkommen in Aussicht gestellt, das nicht nur die Ukraine, sondern möglicherweise »ganz Europa« betreffen könnte. »Es wird mehr als die Ukraine umfassen, und ich könnte sogar sagen, dass es ganz Europa umfassen könnte«, sagte Trump vor Journalisten im Oval Office.
Kremlberater Kirill Dmitrijew und Trump-Berater Steve Witkoff
Foto: Vyacheslav Prokofyev / Sputnik Kremlin / AP / dpa
Nach einem von seiner Frau Melania Trump veranstalteten Treffen von Vertretern Moskaus und Kyjiws im Weißen Haus traf der US-Präsident am Donnerstag nach eigenen Angaben mit Kremlberater Kirill Dmitrijew zusammen. Ukrainische Vertreter empfing er dagegen nicht zu einem Gespräch.
Neue Befürchtungen in Europa
»Ich kann Ihnen nicht sagen, worüber ich gesprochen habe«, sagte Trump nach seinem Treffen mit dem Berater des russischen Präsidenten Wladimir Putin. »Ich sage Ihnen nur: Es wird eine Übereinkunft geben, es wird eine große Übereinkunft geben.« Er fügte hinzu: »Es wird ein großes, schönes Abkommen werden, und alle werden begeistert sein.«
Trumps Ankündigung eines »ganz Europa« und die Ukraine betreffenden Abkommens und ein Treffen mit dem Putin-Berater Dmitrijew dürften in Kyjiw und der EU Befürchtungen verstärken, wonach der US-Präsident mit Blick auf den Ukrainekrieg eine russlandfreundliche Haltung vertritt. Im Oktober hatte Trump vom US-Kongress beschlossene Sanktionen gegen Russland per Dekret auf Eis gelegt und russische Diesellieferungen an die USA angekündigt.
US-First-Lady Melania Trump hatte sich am Donnerstag bei einem Treffen mit Dmitrijew und dem ukrainischen Unterhändler David Arachamia für eine »dauerhafte« Waffenruhe in der Ukraine ausgesprochen. Als Vorbild könne die sechstägige Feuerpause in der Stadt Oleschky in der vergangenen Woche dienen, sagte die Frau von US-Präsident Trump.
Kremlmann Kirill Dmitrijew mit Melania Trump
Foto: Alex Brandon / AP / dpa
»Jetzt müssen wir den Mut, den wir nach Oleschky gebracht haben, nutzen, um durch das gemeinsame Mitgefühl für das Leid unschuldiger Menschen eine Basis des Einvernehmens zu finden«, sagte sie vor Journalisten. »Gemeinsam können wir etwas schaffen, das dauerhafter ist als eine vorübergehende Waffenruhe.«
Die aus Slowenien stammende Melania Trump erklärte, sie habe Dmitrijew und Arachamia Briefe an den russischen Präsidenten Wladimir Putin und den ukrainischen Staatschef Wolodymyr Selenskyj übergeben. Moskaus Vertreter Dmitrijew erklärte, er habe sich im Namen Putins bei der US-First-Lady für ihre »herausragende humanitäre Rolle« bedankt.
Selenskyj hatte Melania Trump am Mittwoch wegen ihrer Bemühungen um Oleschky mit einem nationalen Orden ausgezeichnet. Er würdige damit ihren »bedeutenden persönlichen Beitrag zur humanitären Unterstützung für die Ukraine sowie ihr aktives Engagement für Menschenrechte und Wohltätigkeit«, erklärte das Präsidentenbüro in Kyjiw.
Die First Lady hatte die begrenzte Waffenruhe in der russisch besetzten ukrainischen Stadt Oleschky vermittelt, um einen humanitären Einsatz zu ermöglichen. Die Feuerpause, die bis Sonntag galt, war die längste in dem seit gut viereinhalb Jahren andauernden Angriffskrieg Russlands gegen die Ukraine. Melania Trump hatte sich in der Vergangenheit mehrfach für die Rückkehr nach Russland verschleppter ukrainischer Kinder eingesetzt.
Am Dienstag und Mittwoch kommender Woche kommen Unterhändler Russlands, der Ukraine und der USA in Abu Dhabi zu Dreiergesprächen über ein mögliches Ende des Ukrainekriegs zusammen. Es ist das erste derartige Treffen seit Februar. Im Vorfeld hatte der ukrainische Präsident Selenskyj in Kyjiw Gespräche mit den US-Sondergesandten Steve Witkoff und Jared Kushner geführt.

A135.text:
Verhandlungen über Ukrainekonflikt Meloni fordert europäische Einigkeit nach Putin-Telefonat
Die italienische Ministerpräsidentin Giorgia Meloni fordert eine verbindliche Entscheidung darüber, wer Europa bei Verhandlungen über ein Ende des Ukrainekriegs vertritt. »Was ich weiterhin fordere, ist, dass ein für alle Mal entschieden wird, wer am Verhandlungstisch im Namen der Europäischen Union sitzt und mit welchem Mandat«, schrieb Meloni in einem Brief an EU-Ratspräsident António Costa.
Die italienische Regierungschefin erklärte, ein »uneinheitliches Vorgehen mit Initiativen, die sich gegenseitig jagen und überschneiden«, werde Europa »weder bei unseren Partnern helfen noch bei jenen, die wir davon überzeugen müssen, eine sinnlose Aggression zu beenden«.
Meloni fordert Entscheidung kommende Woche
Beim nächsten informellen Europäischen Rat in Dublin kommende Woche solle diese Frage unter den Partnern erörtert werden, forderte Meloni in dem Schreiben. Der Europäische Rat am 17. und 18. Dezember in Brüssel wiederum soll dadurch in der Lage sein, »nach einer Abstimmung mit dem Vereinigten Königreich, Norwegen und den anderen interessierten europäischen Partnern eine entsprechende Entscheidung förmlich zu beschließen«.
Sollte keine Einigung auf eine gemeinsame Stimme gelingen, drohe Europa im Verhandlungsprozess die Bedeutungslosigkeit, warnte Meloni. Sie erklärte, man gebe sonst weiter das Bild eines Europas ab, das uneinheitlich vorgehe. Dies diene den Interessen jener, die wollen, dass dieser Krieg weitergeht. »Und ich halte das für inakzeptabel, angesichts der Tatsache, dass Menschenleben und die Zukunft unserer Sicherheit auf dem Spiel stehen.«
Costa reagierte prompt. Noch am Abend dankte er Meloni, dass sie ihre Bedenken so klar dargelegt habe, und erklärte sich zum Handeln bereit. »Ich nehme Ihre Bitte zur Kenntnis, diese Angelegenheit auf der bevorstehenden informellen Tagung des Europäischen Rates in Dublin weiter zu erörtern, und werde Zeit für diese Diskussion einplanen«, hieß es in seiner Antwort.
Meloni hatte sich bereits in der Vergangenheit mehrfach kritisch über einzelne Initiativen und Gesprächsformate gezeigt, die ihrer Ansicht nach zu einer Zersplitterung der europäischen Position im Ukrainekrieg beitragen. Zuletzt gab es aus Rom Kritik an dem unter den Europäern nicht koordinierten Telefonat von Finnlands Präsident Alexander Stubb und Norwegens Regierungschef Jonas Gahr Støre mit Kremlchef Wladimir Putin Ende Oktober.
Beide hatten ihre Initiative mit einem Wunsch Kyjiws begründet. Stubb gilt seit Längerem als einer der wenigen Europäer, denen sowohl der ukrainische Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj als auch US-Präsident Donald Trump Gehör schenken. Auch Meloni wurde diese Stellung immer wieder nachgesagt.

A138.text:
Keinen Monat nach Eingriff Papst beginnt trotz Krebs-OP seine Südamerikareise
Es ist keinen Monat her, dass sich Papst Leo XIV. einer Krebs-Operation an der Lunge unterzogen hat. Trotzdem ist er nun zu einer zwölftägigen Reise nach Südamerika aufgebrochen, es soll sein bislang längster Trip werden.
Erste Station ist Uruguay. Dort soll das Oberhaupt von weltweit 1,4 Milliarden Katholiken in der Hauptstadt Montevideo von Präsident Yamandu Orsi empfangen werden. Weitere Stationen sind das Nachbarland Argentinien sowie Peru. Für den Pontifex ist es eine Rückkehr: In dem Andenstaat verbrachte Leo mehr als 20 Jahre als Missionar für den Augustinerorden und dann als Bischof. Der gebürtige US-Amerikaner hat seither auch die peruanische Staatsbürgerschaft.
Ärzte erklären Papst für gesund
Wegen seiner Krebserkrankung hatte es in den vergangenen Wochen Zweifel gegeben, ob der 71-Jährige die Reise überhaupt antreten kann. Das Kirchenoberhaupt hatte sich erst am 13. Oktober einer Lungenkrebs-Operation unterzogen. Dabei war ihm ein Teil des rechten Lungenflügels mit einem bösartigen Tumor entfernt worden. Trotz der Sorge um den Papst gaben die behandelnden Ärzte jetzt jedoch grünes Licht. Nach Angaben der Ärzte ist Leo wieder krebsfrei.
Frau mit Papstbild in Peru
Foto: Jao Yamunaque / dpa
Das Programm der Reise soll nach Angaben des Vatikans unverändert bleiben. Neben zahlreichen Begegnungen mit Vertretern aus Politik, Religion und Zivilgesellschaft sowie Gottesdiensten ist auch ein Ausflug auf etwa 3700 Metern Höhe in die peruanischen Anden geplant.
Auch in Heimat von Vorgänger Franziskus
In Südamerika ist der Anteil der Katholiken deutlich höher als in Europa. Anders als in den beiden späteren Besuchsländern gilt in Uruguay eine strikte Trennung zwischen Kirche und Staat. Argentinien war die Heimat von Leos Vorgänger, des vergangenes Jahr an Ostern verstorbenen Papstes Franziskus. Als Pontifex kehrte Franziskus nie dorthin zurück.
Sowohl Argentinien als auch Peru werden von rechtspopulistischen Staatschefs regiert, Präsident Javier Milei und Präsidentin Keiko Fujimori. Bei mehr als 50 Terminen sind allein 36 Ansprachen des Papstes geplant. In Rom wird der Papst am 17. November zurückerwartet.

A14.text:
Why is Iran exempting India, China, Qatar, Iraq from Hormuz restrictions?
Tehran says ships from four countries can cross Hormuz freely, but analysts say the deals carry political risks.
Iran has exempted ships from India, China, Iraq and Qatar from its Strait of Hormuz restrictions, a senior Iranian lawmaker said on Tuesday.
“Ships from these countries pass freely, and the Americans do not intercept them either,” Amir Hayat Moqaddam, deputy chairman of the Iranian parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, told the Iranian Students’ News Agency (ISNA).
Iran effectively shut the strait early in the US-Israel war on Iran, which began on February 28, and the United States reimposed a naval blockade on Iran’s southern ports in July.
So why have these four countries been granted passage through the critical strait, and can their ships really sail freely while the blockade remains in place?
What does Iran get in return for letting ships pass?
It will receive medicine from India and political backing from China, according to Hayat Moqaddam. Iran already receives diplomatic support from Qatar, which is leading mediation efforts to end the US-Israel war on Iran.
Hayat Moqaddam said Tehran will also collect transit fees from Indian and Chinese ships, while Qatari vessels pass free. He did not say whether Iraqi ships will pay a toll.
“Whatever the lawmaker says is the rationale – the big question is if it works and, if yes, to what extent?” Rouzbeh Parsi, an Iran analyst and affiliated researcher at Lund University’s Department of History and Human Rights Studies, told Al Jazeera.
“Iran has been under sanctions for a very long time, so bartering and quid pro quos in trade are nothing new,” he said. The difference now, he added, is that “it’s about poking holes in an embargo and getting crucial goods/services in and out”.
Nader Hashemi, an associate professor of Middle East politics at Georgetown University, said that “most likely Iran is charging a transit fee or a percentage of the cargo value to allow those ships to go through without being harassed”.
“It’s a clever move by Tehran for several reasons,” Wolfgang Pusztai, a security and defence analyst and Austria’s former defence attache to Libya, told Al Jazeera.
“If successful, this move will generate significant revenue for Iran, as China is by far the largest purchaser of Iranian crude oil, buying nearly 90 percent of Iran’s total oil exports,” he said.
By including Qatar, with its many liquefied natural gas (LNG) buyers, and India, Iran is also “trying to undermine acceptance” of Washington’s strategy in the conflict, especially as it charges Qatar no tolls, he added.
Why does it matter to these four countries?
All four are highly dependent on the Strait of Hormuz for exports.
Of the 10.23 million barrels a day of Gulf crude that passed through the strait in October, about 42 percent went to China and 13 percent to India, Muyu Xu, a senior crude oil analyst at the analytics firm Kpler, told Al Jazeera.
“China is the country most able to cross US interests. The question is whether Beijing considers it worth the potential political cost,” Parsi said.
Asia is particularly reliant on Gulf oil and gas usually shipped out via Hormuz. Countries there have much to offer in return for allowing ships to pass.
“For India, the shutdown of oil from the Gulf has been a great loss – and it is a big producer of the pharmaceuticals that Iran cannot manufacture itself,” he said.
Qatar, which is mediating between Washington and Tehran, shipped no LNG through the strait in August, but managed 1.8 million tonnes in October, Xu said.
Its crude transits fell over the same period, from 517,000 barrels a day to 193,000, while Iraq’s rose from 1.69 million to 2.65 million.
Kpler has been unable to trace the origin of up to two million barrels a day of Middle Eastern crude, so both countries’ flows may be higher, Xu said.
[truncated]

Tech stock rout, driven by US AI fears, continues in Asian trading
Global markets roiled due to concerns that US midterm election results will lead to slowing data centre expansion and increased regulation of AI.
A tech stock rout that began overnight in the United States has persisted in Asian trading.
Market authorities in South Korea paused trading on Friday as prices plunged across the region. Global markets have been rattled by a sharp fall in the trading price of tech stocks, which is driven by fears that the Democrats’ victory in the US midterm elections will increase regulatory scrutiny of AI and slow the country’s data centre build-out.
Japan’s Nikkei index slumped 6 percent, its deepest one-day drop since April 2025. Indices in South Korea and Taiwan plunged more than 8 percent after the opening bell, before cutting losses as authorities scrambled to stem the selling.
Wall Street’s volatility “fear gauge” soared overnight on Thursday and the tech-focused Nasdaq sank 5.5 percent, wiping $3 trillion off S&P 500 firms, as investors fretted that the Democrats could put the brakes on the AI boom being encouraged by President Donald Trump.
“It was a brutal morning for many investors here in Asia. We saw that the AI sell-off continues here across many countries,” Al Jazeera’s Katrina Yu reported from Beijing.
“Some of those major markets have fortunately recovered some of those losses, but all of them are still clearly in the red,” she said.
Analysts say the political jitters are hitting an AI trade already on shaky footing due to worries about returns on massive spending on related infrastructure.
“The selloff shows that AI stock prices had been built on rosy illusions about the future, and now that illusion is gone,” Dong Baozhen, chairman of asset manager Lingtong Shengtai, told the Reuters news agency.
“The US stock market has been the standard-bearer and backbone of the global AI bull run. Now that backbone has snapped. Can AI bull markets elsewhere hold up on their own?”
Authorities step in
Markets cut some of their losses by the time Asian markets closed, as authorities worked to stem the panic.
Trading on South Korea’s Kospi market was temporarily halted amid the sharp slide. Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il also eased rules on retail investors’ leveraged investments.
In China, state entities stepped in to buy up equities in a bid to stabilise the market, said Al Jazeera’s Yu.
The Taiwan stock market closed down 4.5 percent, recovering somewhat from its early morning slump. For the week, the index clocked a 12.2 percent decline, its biggest since 1991, LSEG data showed.
The government of the island state, a key producer of chips, sought to talk up the prospects for the sector.
Demand for emerging technologies like AI, high-performance computing and cloud services is expected to keep expanding, driving demand for tech companies, the economy ministry said in a statement issued on Friday.
Korean AI chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix fell nearly 6 percent and 9.4 percent respectively, cutting steep losses from earlier. TSMC fell as much as 8.5 percent in Taiwan, before closing down 4.7 percent.
In Japan, Kioxia plunged 11 percent while AI investor SoftBank Group slid 11 percent.
New regulations
The selling indicates investors are starting to factor in increased opposition to data centres. Analysts say markets have yet to fully consider the cost such building work has imposed on communities.
Toby Walsh, the chief scientist for the AI Institute at Australia’s University of New South Wales, said he expected new regulations on data centres in many countries, including the US, Australia and the United Kingdom.
“The developers were building them in a way that wasn’t actually getting social licence,” Walsh told Al Jazeera.
“They were building them in places where they didn’t need to build. You don’t have to build data centres in urban areas. You can build them in the middle of nowhere.

Iran’s security chief meets Putin, delivers message from Khamenei
Putin meets Iran’s top security official to discuss regional security and receives a letter from Mojtaba Khamenei.
Russia’s President Vladimir Putin has met Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei in Moscow to discuss regional security as diplomatic efforts gather pace to end the United States and Israel’s war on Iran.
During the meeting on Thursday, Rezaei also delivered a letter to Putin from Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, according to the Iranian state broadcaster Press TV.
Speaking after the meeting, Rezaei said the talks had focused on security arrangements in the region, as well as Russia’s support for ending what he called the US’s “aggression” against Iran.
“Important regional issues were discussed with Putin and significant conversations took place regarding the post-war period and regional security arrangements,” he said.
Other topics, he said, included plans to deepen energy cooperation, including building gas pipelines from Russia to Iran.
Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said Khamenei had wanted him to deliver the message to Putin as soon as possible. The trip to Moscow had been planned nearly a month earlier, he said, but was postponed due to “daily discussions about the military situation in the region”.
He did not say what the message contained.
Khamenei said in a written statement on Wednesday that there should not be “even the slightest inclination towards submission” to the US. He also called for an “ever stronger” Iran to reach a “point of absolute deterrence”.
Seven conditions
Rezaei’s meeting with Putin came as Qatar steps up diplomatic efforts to end the war on Iran amid fears the US could renew attacks following its midterm elections.
In Tuesday’s vote, US President Donald Trump’s Republican Party lost control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate amid widespread anger over rising prices that many blame on the war on Iran.
Efforts to end the conflict have centred on the future status of the strategic Strait of Hormuz, a US blockade of Iranian ports, sanctions against Iran, and a resumption of negotiations over the country’s nuclear programme.
Rezaei said on Thursday that Tehran would not hold talks with the US on ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz until Washington meets its seven demands.
“On the issue of diplomacy, we have announced seven conditions to the Americans. As long as they do not execute our seven conditions, we will neither open the Strait of Hormuz nor have negotiations,” he said.
According to Rezaei, Putin reiterated that Russia is ready to provide support to end the war. Last month, Putin told Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian that Russia was prepared to “do everything” it could towards that end, Russian news agencies reported.
Rezaei said the discussion at the Kremlin also focused on the construction of a gas pipeline from Russia to Iran, aimed at addressing Iran’s gas shortages and enabling Russia to sell its gas to countries neighbouring Iran.
He added that he had briefed Putin on a meeting held in Tehran in late October among Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan, and that the Russian leader had welcomed it.
“Like our Chinese friends, we believe that there should be regional arrangements and that foreign countries should not interfere in the security of the region,” he said.
The Kremlin did not immediately release its own account of the meeting, which took place in the Senate Palace, according to Russia’s TASS news agency.
Separately, Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi held phone calls with his counterparts in Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Oman, Qatar, Turkiye and Jordan.
His calls focused on regional developments and ongoing diplomatic efforts to promote peace, Iranian state media reported.
Russia and Iran, both under heavy Western sanctions, have strengthened their diplomatic and military ties in recent years.

A28.text:
Israel faces new era of sinking US support after election
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's brash campaign posters are still up on Israeli public buses -- images of him, US President Donald Trump and soaring warjets that laud the two leaders attacking Iran together.
Neither is now advertising the state of the two countries' alliance.
A week after an inconclusive election for Netanyahu, Americans overwhelmingly rejected Trump and chose a Congress led by Democrats who want a tougher approach to Israel, whether on Iran, Gaza or settler violence in the occupied West Bank.
The back-to-back elections look to many observers like a turning point, with Israel no longer able to take for granted the cover of the world's most powerful country.
"This is a new era. The confluence of the Gaza war and the war with Iran have really changed how mainstream Americans -- not people particularly concerned with the Israeli-Palestinian conflict -- see Israel," said Yael Sternhell, an expert on the United States at Tel Aviv University.
Vice President JD Vance, assessing why his Republicans fared poorly, listed four ways to bring voters back, including ending the Iran war and changing "our relationship with Israel".
Trump did not disagree. Just as voting was underway Tuesday, Trump said he had agreed with Netanyahu to end the $3.8 billion in annual US military aid to Israel by the end of this year, explicitly tying the decision to the US political mood.
Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister who has served on and off for nearly two decades, had eagerly sought Trump's endorsement but also acknowledged his country's growing isolation.
In the final days of the campaign, he suggested Israel turn to cryptocurrencies to circumvent international sanctions he expected would intensify.
Netanyahu has not commented on the US election or Trump's aid remarks.
Amit Segal, a journalist known for his proximity to Netanyahu, posted that the political situation in the United States marked a "catastrophe" for Israel.
- Can Eisenkot restore the alliance? -
Opposition contender Gadi Eisenkot, who is trying to cobble together a coalition to oust Netanyahu, has cast himself as capable of repairing relations.
In an English-language statement, the former military chief said he believed in "liberal values" and also wanted to work "closely and constructively" with Trump.
Yair Golan, the main left-wing leader inside Eisenkot's bloc, called for Israel to restore a bipartisan approach destroyed by Netanyahu who he said promoted a "destructive Israeli narrative of eternal war and authoritarian rule".
Netanyahu boasted in his campaign about standing up to Democratic presidents including Barack Obama, who remains a hero for many Democrats. Netanyahu openly aligned with Republicans a decade ago to attack Obama's diplomacy on Iran.
"Netanyahu certainly rubs Democrats the wrong way and has made every effort to alienate them," Sternhell said.
"But Eisenkot can't just be a nicer man to receive a softer approach from this new Congress," she added. "He's going to need new policies."
She said Eisenkot would likely enjoy Israeli public support for cracking down on extremist settlers, who have attacked Palestinians in the West Bank with virtual impunity.
But Israel has shifted to the right, with wide initial support for the Gaza war.
- Broadening criticism of Israel -
The new Congress will include progressive Democrats such as Abdul El-Sayed, the first Muslim elected to the Senate, who describe the devastation in Gaza as genocide, an assertion rejected by Israel.
Netanyahu "made a bet not only on the Republicans but almost personally on Trump", said Eli Kowaz, senior policy director of the Economic Cooperation Foundation, an Israeli think tank that backs a two-state solution with the Palestinians.
"These results show that bet had an expiry date," Kowaz said. "Also, for the first time, really, I think there's a realisation that it isn't only about the Democrats.

A31.text:
Analysis-Midterms upended Congress but Trump still commands foreign policy
By Matt Spetalnick
WASHINGTON, Nov 5 (Reuters) - The Republican Party's staggering losses at the ballot box this week have left President Donald Trump diminished in Washington and facing tougher legislative oversight and scrutiny of his agenda.
But on foreign policy, he could remain unbowed.
Even as Democratic lawmakers seek to rein in the Republican president when they take control of Congress, Trump will retain broad latitude to pursue his objectives on the world stage, from Iran and Israel to Ukraine and China, during his final two years in office.
The central question, analysts say, is whether Trump will feel chastened by his party’s poor showing in Tuesday’s midterm elections or emboldened to take more dramatic steps to craft his legacy in US relations with friends and foes alike.
Most urgent is the intractable war against Iran, which Trump acknowledged on Wednesday contributed to his party losing both chambers of Congress. He insisted, though, he had no regrets about attacking the Islamic Republic and it was essential to stop Tehran from acquiring a nuclear weapon, which it says it has never sought.
The midterms outcome illustrated voter backlash after eight months of conflict that have driven US gasoline prices up and his approval ratings down.
Democrats had accused Republicans of ceding Congress’ war-making powers and giving Trump a free hand internationally, not just against Iran but with his approach to Russia’s war in Ukraine, his tariffs campaign, his capture of Venezuela’s president, and deadly boat strikes off Latin America.
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer told reporters on Wednesday his party's mandate is to put a check on “Trump's chaos at home and abroad” and end the Iran war.
That is easier said than done, given the extensive leeway with foreign policy and military operations that presidents have long possessed.
“A Democratic Congress has the ability to stop Trump's domestic legislative agenda, but it doesn't have much ability to stop a president from exercising his powers as commander-in-chief,” said William Wechsler, senior director of Middle East programs at the Atlantic Council.
Democrats’ main tools could be investigations, Trump nominees' confirmation hearings and funding authority to curb his foreign operations, but analysts say their leverage will be limited.
While not responding directly to Reuters' questions about the election's implications, White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said: “President Trump has effectively restored American strength on the global stage ... The president will continue to work with anyone to put America first and improve the livelihoods of families across the country, and his foreign policy decisions have never been motivated by politics."
FACING LAME-DUCK STATUS
Presidents entering their lame-duck phase, when barred from running again and seeing influence waning at home, have often focused on global affairs – and many analysts expect something similar from Trump.
But some experts see the risk of Trump’s impulsiveness leading to further instability in the Middle East or sparking conflict elsewhere, possibly targeting Cuba, a Communist-ruled island he has placed under an oil blockade and repeatedly threatened.
“If triggered and cornered," said Laura Blumenfeld, a foreign policy analyst at Johns Hopkins University, "Trump may elect to flex his presidential powers through unilateral use of force abroad.”
With Iran, Trump faces the choice of launching a new round of airstrikes, seeking a negotiated exit or maintaining the status quo - a tense stalemate keeping global energy prices high and Gulf neighbors on edge.
While Iranian leaders have gloated over what they see as Trump’s humiliation at home, people in Washington familiar with the deliberations say he could still take military action. One source said Trump had nothing to lose politically now.
[truncated]

A32.text:
Why China stands to gain from Trump's midterm drubbing
Beijing can now portray its diplomatic backing, purchases of Iranian oil and provision of dual-use technology as having helped Iran withstand a war that has exacted a political price from the US president.
You're reading an excerpt from Al-Monitor China-Middle East, where we analyze China's deepening engagement with the region. To get this newsletter in your inbox weekly, sign up here.
WASHINGTON – Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress, with Democrats securing at least 54 Senate seats and a projected House majority of between 251 and 268 seats. Upsets in Texas, Kansas and South Carolina underscored the historic nature of the election.
When the new Congress convenes in January, as Elizabeth Hagedorn reports, Trump will confront an opposition empowered to investigate his administration, challenge spending priorities and obstruct his legislative agenda. Much of it will center on the Middle East, the US-Iran war, and business ties and deals with Gulf monarchies forged over the past two years by Trump officials or people in the president’s orbit.
For Beijing, that creates an opportunity. A president facing domestic paralysis may become more invested in securing an agreement abroad, particularly one he can sell as relief for US consumers. Chinese negotiators could conclude that Trump needs a deal more urgently than they do.
Iran’s political price
The clearest opening concerns Iran. Vice President JD Vance blamed the war for the Republican defeat, while Trump acknowledged that its impact on energy prices contributed to the losses, even as he defended the decision to fight.
The election was not an endorsement of China’s foreign policy, but it gives Beijing political ammunition to argue that negotiations, rather than renewed military escalation, offer the better route out of the conflict and to defend its sustained support for Tehran. Beijing can now portray its diplomatic backing, purchases of Iranian oil and provision of dual-use technology as having helped Iran withstand a war that has exacted a political price from the US president.
More room in the Gulf
China was already expanding its regional diplomacy before the election. This week, as Beatrice Farhat reported, Xi hosted Oman’s sultan, while Foreign Minister Wang Yi held separate talks with senior Iranian and Saudi officials. Beijing also announced plans to dispatch its Middle East envoy to those three countries.
A politically bruised Trump could make that diplomatic pitch more compelling. Beijing can present itself as focused on negotiations, restored shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and economic stability, while Washington wrestles with a stubborn Iranian negotiating team.
A humbled Trump
Trump will arrive at his meeting with Xi politically weakened at home and under pressure to deliver economic relief. Unlike in previous elections, when he invoked allegations of fraud to challenge the results, Trump was quick to acknowledge the outcome. “I don’t want to be just sitting there for two years vetoing everything,” he told Politico.
The results will make him even more inclined to work with China and avoid an economic breakdown. The trade truce expires in January. Extending it would help avert another round of tariffs, retaliatory measures and uncertainty for businesses. Lowering tariffs could ease import costs, but securing a durable agreement requires China’s cooperation and gives Beijing an opening to demand concessions in return.
That is Xi’s leverage: Trump needs a deal he can sell at home, while China can bargain over its price.
But a weaker Trump does not mean a more accommodating US Congress. The incoming majority could press the White House to release stalled arms sales to Taiwan, intensify scrutiny of Chinese investments and challenge Beijing over human rights. China may gain leverage with the president only to face a more confrontational Congress on issues it considers especially sensitive.

A5.text:
Can America ever return to pre-Trump politics?
The US midterms were a rejection of Donald Trump’s politics of division, but his legacy may be impossible to undo.
“I think it’s safe to say that we are tired of being pitted against each other. We are tired of being told to hate each other. It has been 10 years of this kind of politics. Politics as blood sport. Politics as trolling and owning. Politics as professional wrestling. It tears families apart. It ends friendships, and it leaves us all feeling terrible all the time.”
So said Senator-elect James Talarico in his victory speech on election night after he won the first United States Senate seat in Texas for the Democratic Party in almost 40 years.
I don’t like Talarico or his policies, but I agree with him on one thing: The American people are tired of being pitted against one another. We need more uniters and fewer dividers in the Republican Party and US politics in general.
This is the conclusion many American voters seem to have reached after 10 years of Donald Trump dominating the right.
A decade ago, he forcefully entered the political scene with a radically different approach and provocative rhetoric. He won his first US presidential election by attacking his opponents with clever and cutting nicknames. Crooked Hillary. Low-energy Jeb. Pocahontas. Little Marco. Crazy Bernie. Lying Ted.
All were aimed at diminishing his rivals in ways that only a rapturous crowd of adoring MAGA fans could really appreciate. His attacks played well on social media and reflected an American culture that was far less deferential to the political establishment, far coarser in its language and far more interested in being entertained than being informed.
Trump’s attacks, performed live at his raucous rallies, had all the earmarks of a professional wrestling bout. It was blood sport at its most basic level. And Trump’s supporters ate it up, loving how he stood up to an elite that obviously despised them.
His opponent in the 2016 presidential election, Hillary Clinton, called half of his supporters a “basket of deplorables”.
Seven years before Trump formally entered the race for the White House, Barack Obama in a speech in San Francisco had said that people like them “get bitter, they cling to guns or religion or antipathy to people who aren’t like them or anti-immigrant sentiment or anti-trade sentiment as a way to explain their frustrations”.
Trump gathered up these angry voters, many of whom had protested during the Tea Party movement, and created “Make America Great Again” (MAGA). They loved the visceral way Trump communicated. They loved that he promised to end illegal immigration and free-trade policies that destroyed manufacturing jobs.
Trump’s rhetoric, coarse as it was, seemed honest, authentic, unscripted, and totally real, not poll-tested, not AI-generated, not written by expensive speechwriters. Trump was talking to them, not at them. He had listened to their fears and promised to fight back with a vengeance.
When Trump claimed the political establishment had stolen his re-election, he didn’t sit idly by, accepting the results. He consulted his lawyers, came up with a dubious legal strategy and then unleashed his supporters on Capitol Hill, hoping upon hope that their pressure would bend the hallowed traditions of presidential succession to his will. It didn’t work, but it also didn’t disqualify him.
Over the four years of President Joe Biden’s administration, Trump survived legal attacks, threats of imprisonment and assassination attempts to become an invincible force who seized power again in 2024. His ascent seemed like destiny.
But as it often does, the fickle winds of the electorate changed direction. They used to love his unconventional approach to politics, but now they wanted him to deliver on his promises to lower inflation and gas prices. He had once promised to keep us out of foreign wars, but that promise was broken, too.

The fifth plenum of the Chinese Communist Party’s Central Committee, which closed on October 29, was not called to make appointments. It still said a good deal about who is on the way up and who is finished. Those who failed to turn up can be written off, while changes in rank, and even new faces in the room, show who is being groomed.
Promotion in the CCP follows a ladder. Members of the Politburo’s Standing Committee, the top echelon of power, are drawn from the previous Politburo, and Politburo members usually come from the Central Committee, while the party constitution stipulates that vacancies on the committee go to alternate members in the order of the votes they received. An official who gets onto the ladder early has the best chance of reaching the top.
Barring sudden illness, an empty seat at a plenum points to chronic ill health or political trouble. The committee elected in 2022 had 205 full members and 171 alternates; only 162 full members and 117 alternates turned up this time. The plenum confirmed the expulsion of 33 people, including Zhang Youxia, once Xi Jinping’s most senior general. Together with earlier casualties – such as two members of the military commission, He Weidong and Miao Hua, and the former foreign minister Qin Gang, who quit the committee in 2024 – that brings the number removed to 37 full members and 15 alternates.
Nearly 20 more full members stayed away from the plenum, though only three are formally under investigation. Among the absentees were Han Jun, who was removed as agriculture minister in April, the navy commander, Hu Zhongming, and the air force’s political commissar, Guo Puxiao. All three are probably finished.
The plenum promoted just one man: Zhang Shengmin, the sole remaining vice chair of the Central Military Commission (CMC), who joined the Politburo. Vice chairs normally sit there, but when Zhang Shengmin was appointed a year ago, Zhang Youxia still represented the military, so his elevation could wait.
The delay may well have been a ruse. Xi was probably already planning to move against Zhang Youxia, and putting Zhang Shengmin on the Politburo then might have tipped him off. Making Zhang Shengmin vice chair and nothing more kept Zhang Youxia at ease.
Zhang Youxia’s fall left the armed forces with no one on the Politburo. The military is a vast interest group, and if it has no voice at the top, even on policies that touch both soldiers and civilians, resentment builds in the ranks. Zhang Shengmin’s promotion fills that gap and shows how much Xi now leans on him; it also explains why nobody else moved up.
Xinjiang’s party chief usually sits on the Politburo, yet Chen Xiaojiang did not inherit the seat vacated by his expelled predecessor, Ma Xingrui. However sensitive Xinjiang is, it is still a province, and for now it ranks below the army. Chen will probably get his seat at next year’s party congress.
Nor did the CMC, whose membership requires a plenum’s approval, gain anyone, chiefly because Xi has too few full generals to choose from. Since Xi’s reforms, the commission has comprised Xi as chairman, two vice chairs, the defense minister, the chief of the joint staff, and the heads of political work and military discipline. Apart from Xi’s own, only three of these posts are filled: by Zhang Shengmin; by Dong Jun, the defense minister, whom Xi has long kept at arm’s length; and by Zhang Shuguang, discipline chief only since July. The other full generals have barely settled into their commands. Yang Zhibin and Han Shengyan, who lead the eastern and central theaters, were promoted last December, and Wang Gang, the air force chief, followed in July.
Filling the CMC is urgent, but Xi cannot afford to rush. The many members who missed the plenum without any announcement of their fall suggest that the investigations of the officer corps are far from over, and anyone Xi promotes must be clean, or the high command could collapse again.
[truncated]

A59.text:
Pope begins lengthy trip to Latin America weeks after lung cancer surgery
- Published
Pope Leo XIV is beginning a lengthy trip to Latin America just three weeks after surgery for lung cancer - a tour that includes a much-anticipated "homecoming" to Peru where he was a priest for many years.
The Vatican says no extraordinary measures are being taken in relation to the Pope's health, describing him as a "71-year-old who has undergone an operation" not someone with a "permanent medical condition".
It was Leo himself who revealed last month that doctors had discovered a tumour during a routine scan. The growth was removed along with the lower lobe of his right lung and his medical team then confirmed the cancer had not spread.
At a briefing in Rome ahead of the trip, which takes in Uruguay and Argentina as well as Peru, a spokeswoman stressed that Pope Leo had "fantastic stamina" and was "extremely enthusiastic" about the schedule which he had "personally confirmed... with no changes".
Back on track
"The Vatican's message with this trip is, 'that was a short episode and now we're back on track'," Professor Massimo Faggioli of Villanova University told the BBC, pointing out that the Pope has had a busy return to work since his surgery.
"We have seen him in these last few days making speeches, audiences and so on. He seems in great shape. That was important."
The 12-day tour would be demanding for anyone, though. It incorporates multiple long-haul and local flights and covers thousands of miles from the Amazon to the Andes.
The starting point will be Uruguay, where the number of Catholics has fallen away steeply in recent years and which is getting its first Papal visit in four decades.
Leo then heads for Argentina, homeland of Pope Francis, his predecessor.
"This visit is also a homage to Francis, who didn't make it to Argentina [as pope]," says Father Fernando Laguna, the rector of Santa Maria Addolorata, Argentina's national church in Rome.
"When this visit by Pope Leo was announced, it filled all of our hearts with joy," he told the BBC. "I always thought he would go, despite his illness. I don't think he ever thought of calling it off!"
The priest is installing a big screen inside the church in Rome to allow parishioners to follow all the key moments of the trip from afar. The building is already decked out with posters declaring Pope Leo is welcome in Argentina. "We're waiting for you!", one proclaims.
This leg of the Pope's journey - which includes meetings with heads of state as well as religious events - could be the most politically sensitive. President Javier Milei once called Pope Francis "evil on earth" and a "communist" for promoting a doctrine of social justice to help the poor. In turn, Argentina's bishops have criticised Milei's harsh austerity measures, making sweeping cuts to social spending.
But Milei has already welcomed Pope Leo, writing in a post on X that Argentina awaits "with immense joy". Millions are expected to turn out to greet him.
'Homecoming' to Peru
The highlight of the trip is undoubtedly saved for last, when Pope Leo reaches Peru - described by the Vatican as a return to his roots.
"He knows these streets," is how a spokeswoman put it.
Born in the US, the then Robert Prevost spent almost 20 years in Peru, on and off, and even has Peruvian citizenship. That time is seen as fundamental to shaping his papacy.
His schedule includes a return to the diocese of Chiclayo where he was ordained bishop in 2014 and remained until Francis moved him to the Vatican almost a decade later.
He will also travel to Cusco, former capital of the Inca Empire, to say Mass more than 3,000m above sea level before heading to Pucallpa in the Amazon.
In all three countries, the Vatican says the Pope will have meetings with survivors of clerical sexual abuse - an issue which clouded a 2018 visit to Chile and Peru by his predecessor.

At least 12 other military sites, including missile complexes and air bases, appear to show signs of repairs. New roofs have been built on destroyed buildings at the Kermanshah missile base in western Iran, near the border with Iraq, while damaged buildings and debris have been cleared at the Parchin military complex - which has been repeatedly repaired despite a succession of air strikes - east of the capital.
The excavations near Shahroud could potentially be related to the production of missiles, said Jim Lamson, a former CIA analyst who focused on Iran. He said that because the nearby air base at Shahroud has been targeted multiple times in recent years, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) is probably trying to find ways to move its production facilities underground.
A MAIAR analyst said that Iran has "a pattern of moving infrastructure underground to protect them from further strikes". Mark Mellett, a defence analyst and former head of the Irish military, said the construction of underground facilities had the added benefit of making it "harder for outside observers to assess the extent and operational status".
Speculation has mounted in recent weeks that the US could resume attacks on Iran after the midterm elections held earlier this week. But on Wednesday Vice-President JD Vance cited the war's unpopularity with voters for the Republicans' poor performance in this week's poll, saying that it may have cost his party control of the Senate "for the next 6 years".
At multiple bases across the country, Iranian forces have focused on carrying-out small-scale repairs to complexes which have been heavily damaged by air strikes since the start of the US-Israeli war.
Analysts said that satellite images appear to show that significant construction has been completed at the Taleghan 2 facility at the Parchin military complex, with damaged buildings levelled and the aftermath of attacks on an underground bunker repaired and reinforced with concrete.
At Karaj and Shahroud, satellite images appear to show significant excavation. At Karaj, multiple vehicles were visible in satellite images, while improvements appear to have been carried out to the nearby airbase.
The images from Karaj appear to show "a new portal for an underground facility", said Sam Lair, research analyst at the Foreign Policy Research Institute (FPRI), which has looked extensively into recent developments at Iranian sites.
Analysis from Janes also indicates there appears to be a new facility under construction at Karaj, including tunnel entrances and structures which could indicate an expansion of nearby damaged or destroyed missile bases - or could also be for storage or other purposes.
The construction work is unlikely to be part of an effort to deceive foreign intelligence agencies, said Janes analyst Sean O'Connor. He said such a project "would be costly and may achieve little".
The developments come after repeated assurances from the White House that US-Israeli attacks have depleted the Iranian armed forces, which US President Donald Trump dismissed as a "complete and total mess".
A Pentagon spokesperson previously said that the US had "destroyed up to 90% of Iran's drone, ballistic missile, and naval industrial base" and "significantly degraded" the country's ability to launch drone and missile attacks.

Following this week’s midterms where voters resoundingly voiced their opposition to data center expansion, OpenAI today announced new commitments to communities where it is working on data center projects, including that it won’t use non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) with public officials.
OpenAI is stepping back from NDAs for data center projects
The ChatGPT maker won’t use NDAs with public officials as part of its new data center community commitments.
Many data center projects have come under scrutiny for relying on NDAs to hide discussions between developers and local officials. However, OpenAI says it is now allowing “only narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets, or proprietary or competitively sensitive information.” In October, Amazon announced it would no longer use NDAs with government agencies it works with on data center projects.
OpenAI’s additional commitments include paying “the full cost” of electricity it uses and the “infrastructure needed to serve us.” It will make opportunities for local communities by publishing the jobs it expects to create and by reporting on hiring. And every future “compute campus” (its rebranding phrase for data centers) the company owns and operates will have a “local compact” that includes the commitments and will reflect “local priorities,” OpenAI says.

Perplexity is taking on OpenAI and Anthropic with its own work-focused AI agents. The startup’s new always-on “Teammates” can take on multiple roles within a workspace, while pulling existing projects, skills, and memory from the Perplexity tools you already use.
Perplexity launches its own take on AI agents for work
Like OpenAI’s Dots and Claude Duet, Perplexity’s Teammates can perform an array of tasks while running 24/7.
Teammates integrate with Perplexity Computer, an AI system that can deploy agents on your device to complete tasks. But Perplexity says Teammates “build on top” of Computer by offering the ability to collaborate and complete “ongoing, large-scale work.” You can assign each Teammate different jobs that they can perform simultaneously — much like OpenAI’s Dots and Claude Duet. Perplexity’s take on the feature is much more expensive, however, as it requires a subscription to its $200 / month Max plan.
Perplexity notes that you can keep tabs on Teammates’ progress through individual threads in the Perplexity app, as well as interact with them in Slack. “Over time, we envision every org having hundreds of teammates working for each person,” Perplexity CEO Aravind Srinivas says on X.

A67.text:
Paraguay President Santiago Peña resigns after bank collapse
- Published
Paraguay's President Santiago Peña has announced his resignation following a political crisis sparked by the collapse of a bank linked to him.
"I want to apologise to the people if at any point I failed," he said in a video message on social media. "It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me."
The crisis erupted after Ueno Bank entered an insolvency process, which froze all operations. Lawmakers accused Peña, who was a shareholder until last year in the company that owned the bank, of conflicts of interest and misconduct.
Peña rejected suggestions of impropriety. His resignation came as Paraguay's lower house of congress voted in favour of pursuing an impeachment trial.
Photos taken near Paraguay's Congress building on Thursday show police officers clashing with protesters demanding Peña be removed from office.
Paraguay's congress must approve the resignation of a president. But a special session convened on Thursday to address his resignation was adjourned in favour of continuing with the impeachment process.
Congress has scheduled a special session for Friday, when Peña is expected to present his defence, according to Reuters news agency.
In a post on X, Peña confirmed he would appear for Senate impeachment proceedings, adding that he would do so to "exercise my right to a defence".
He wrote: "I will provide the information requested of me. Citizens deserve to know the truth, without cover-ups and without anyone being above the law."
Peña earlier said his resignation was to protect stability, social peace and democratic institutions.
Ueno Bank has said it has about three million customers, equivalent to about 60% of Paraguay's adult population.
It held pensions and some other public funds and, after its collapse earlier this week, millions could not access their accounts.
The central bank seized the digital lender, and people took to the streets protesting and demanding Peña's resignation.
A new president of the Central Bank of Paraguay has been appointed and Congress has approved a process to pay depositors.
Peña won election in 2023 representing Paraguay's ruling conservative Colorado Party, beating a centre-left challenger.
The Colorado party dropped impeachment proceedings against Vice President Pedro Alliana, who is next in line for the presidency after Peña.

A72.text:
Melania Trump calls for lasting Ukraine truce as she hosts Russian and Ukrainian officials
- Published
US First Lady Melania Trump called for a "more enduring" ceasefire in Ukraine as she welcomed Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House following last week's truce in the southern region of Kherson.
Hundreds of residents of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky facing starvation and constant bombardment were able to evacuate during a six-day ceasefire, which both Moscow and Kyiv credited Trump with brokering.
"The lives of innocent people must transcend the division of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace," she said.
The unusual White House event saw senior Ukrainian and Russian officials meet away from the setting of official US-brokered peace talks they have been holding without success since last year.
The delegations were made up of Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova, as well as Ukrainian MP Davyd Arakhamia and Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev.
The Kremlin envoy also met Donald Trump, the US president later revealed to reporters.
Trump refused to say what they had discussed, but confirmed he had not met the Ukrainian delegation. "There's going to be an agreement," he asserted, "it's going to be a big agreement, and it's going to involve more than Ukraine... and I could even say it might involve all of Europe."
Melania Trump was credited by both delegations at the White House with playing a key though unspecified role in the ceasefire, and all parties conveyed to her the gratitude of the Russian and Ukrainian presidents.
The US first lady said she had "reviewed demining plans, aerial images, assessed roadways, and discussed evacuation routes, hospital access, vehicles, and medical resources" during the truce.
"Last week in Oleshky and neighbouring areas of Kherson, people experienced the simple joys of life for the first time since 2022," Trump said. "They walked down familiar streets without fear of explosions."
She thanked both Volodymyr Zelensky and Vladimir Putin, making no reference to the origins of the war, which began when the Russian president launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and which has caused thousands of civilian casualties and the displacement of millions.
Dmitriev, a businessman and special Putin envoy who has previously represented Moscow during peace talks with Ukraine, thanked the US first lady for "saving and touching so many lives".
"Let us continue making a humanitarian contribution together; this is within our power," Dmitriev said, before gifting Melania Trump a framed drawing by an 11-year-old Oleshky evacuee.
He also praised Trump for her work on reuniting children separated from their families by the war. These include children allegedly abducted by Russia.
Arakhamia, a Ukrainian MP who heads Zelensky's party in parliament who has also been part of the Ukrainian negotiating team, said the Oleshky ceasefire had constituted the "biggest de-escalation since 2022".
"We are creating a momentum where both sides are learning the… mechanics of how to actually keep the peace when the peace comes," he added.
He acknowledged that the "political track" of negotiations to end the conflict was "complex" but said Ukrainians were asking Melania Trump "to keep going and find new missions and de-escalate more."
At the end of the event, Trump handed Dmitriev and Arakhamia two letters to be hand-delivered to their respective presidents.
The White House later said Melania Trump had invited her guests to view two historic artifacts which she had "personally selected as powerful symbols of peace".
One was an 18th Century medicine chest which was removed from the White House when the British set it on fire in 1812. "Once adversaries, the United States and Great Britain ultimately established a strong alliance," the White House said.

A80.text:
Politics·New
Republicans ran away from Trump's Canadian tariffs, but not far enough
Democrats say they're ready to move quickly to try to end the trade war with Canada
When wildfires were burning across Canada in July, and the smoke was blowing into the United States, Michigan's Mike Rogers was among those demanding punishment.
The Republican senator, echoing U.S. President Donald Trump, said Canada should pay more, on top of the current tariffs, to cover the cost of that pollution.
"Canada must be held accountable for endangering Americans, and I will work with your administration to ensure they are!," he wrote on X, in a reply to Trump.
Rogers had, separately, enthused about the tariffs — telling Fox News they were "really positive" for the U.S. and that it was "absolutely unacceptable" for Canada to be selling cars into his border state.
Fast forward three months and Rogers — struggling in race for Senate — tried to cast himself as a friend of Canada.
While drinking a Labatt Blue and alluding to hockey, he called for an end to the tariffs in an ad posted four weeks ago.
"Here in Michigan, we know that Canada is not our enemy," he said.
A man votes in the primary election at Northwestern High School in Detroit, on Aug. 4. (Nic Antaya/The Associated Press)
It was one of many examples of Republicans trying to distance themselves from Trump’s trade war and anti-Canadian rhetoric.
Now, according to reporting from the Wall Street Journal, the Democrats are hoping to use Republican discomfort with the cross-border trade war to end tariffs on Canada.
Democratic push to end trade war
“There is overwhelming support for repealing the tariffs on products from Canada,” Oregon Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden, ranking member of the Senate Finance Committee, told the WSJ on Wednesday.
Wyden and other Democrats believed they might be able to flip enough Republicans against Trump on the issue to override a veto, the Journal reported. That would likely require persuading about 30 to 35 Republican House members, and 11 to 13 Republican senators, the precise number depending on votes yet to be tallied from Tuesday's elections.
The new House and Senate will be seated on January 3, just two days after punishing 50 per cent tariffs on all Canadian cars, trucks, automotive parts, and steel are scheduled to take effect.
Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who defeated Rogers in Michigan, told the MS Now morning show on Thursday he was keen to work to lift the "stupid tariffs on Canada," and later told CNN that ending Trump's "vanity trade war" was a legislative priority for him in Washington.
“There is no economic reason why we are having a tariff war with our biggest trading partner. This has to end.”
That seems to be one of the lessons American politicians will take from the 2026 midterm elections, perhaps with lasting and positive effects for Canada.
From the early days of Trump’s second term, Americans have shown very little interest in picking fights with Canada. Although Trump's verbal attacks on Canada were a staple at rallies throughout October, the issue again failed to catch fire within the MAGA coalition.
Exit polls on Tuesday, according to CNN, found that two-thirds of American voters believed tariffs had hurt both the national and their local economies.
The tariffs were widely seen as having combined with the Iran war to create a double price shock.
Rural America has been hit especially hard by the spike in diesel, which contributed to higher costs for fertilizer. All of the eight main fertilizers used by U.S. farmers cost more than they did a year ago, according to one industry analysis.
Those numbers were key to the massive hemorrhaging of Republican votes in red states such as Kansas.

A85.text:
Business
AI stock sell-off sends the S&P 500 down 4.4% in worst day since April 2025
The S&P 500 saw its worst session since Trump shook markets with his 'Liberation Day' tariffs
A brutal sell-off swept through Wall Street Thursday, led by stocks tied to the buildout of AI data centres. The wipeout more than erased the U.S. stock market's gain from the day before, which was its best in three months.
The S&P 500 fell 4.4 per cent for its worst day since U.S. President Donald Trump shook markets worldwide in April 2025 with his "Liberation Day" tariffs. The Dow Jones Industrial Average sank 1,833 points, or 3.4 per cent, while the Nasdaq Composite tumbled 5.5 per cent.
The Nasdaq, which is full of AI-related and other tech stocks, sank 11.9 per cent below its all-time high set last month. Stock geeks call a loss of more than 10 per cent a "correction."
Canada's main stock index lost 736.13 points at 35,605.27, weighed down by losses in the technology sector. The Canadian dollar traded for 71.48 cents US compared with 71.63 cents US on Wednesday.
Stock markets around the world felt pressure from continued drops for companies that had benefited from the boom in the artificial-intelligence technology industry, and South Korea's Kospi index tumbled 5.3 per cent. Such stocks have been swinging for months on worries that the construction of further AI data centres may slow because of how expensive it's become to borrow money. Critics also said AI stock prices had shot too high and were in a bubble.
U.S. midterm challenges AI investment frenzy
Tuesday's U.S. midterm elections added another challenge. The nationwide victories for Democrats raised the possibility that governments could force pauses in construction of more data centres.
Voters across political parties say they're wary about AI and don't like the increases to power bills caused by data centres.
Any slowdown in construction of AI data centres would mean fewer purchases of AI chips, not to mention electricity and other products and services that are getting vacuumed up in the AI frenzy, which is driving much of the U.S. economy's growth.
Nvidia, the chip company that quickly became the face of the AI boom, fell 9.3 per cent and was by far the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. It's now down 2.6 per cent for the year so far following annual gains of roughly 39 per cent, 171 per cent and 239 per cent in the last three years.
Advanced Micro Devices tumbled 17.3 per cent. CoreWeave, a company that rents access to AI chips to customers over the cloud, fell 9.8 per cent. GE Vernova, which has been helping to power data centres, sank 7.5 per cent.
Compounding the pain for investors, AI chip stocks are some of Wall Street's most influential because they've become some of the largest. A one per cent move for Nvidia, for example, has more effect on the S&P 500 than a one per cent move for nearly any other U.S. stock.
Thursday's losses were broad after gains for the majority of stocks on Wall Street during the morning quickly evaporated.
Among the handful of winners was AppLovin, which jumped 31 per cent after the marketing platform reported both revenue and profit that topped analysts' expectations. The company's board also approved a program to send up to $3.2 billion US to investors by buying back its own stock, bringing the program's total potential value to $3.6 billion US.
Tapestry rallied 7.1 per cent after the company behind the Coach and Kate Spade brands likewise delivered a stronger profit than expected. It also raised its forecasts for revenue and earnings this fiscal year.
All told, the S&P 500 fell 334.89 points to 7,353.73. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1,833.06 to 51,523.06, and the Nasdaq Composite sank 1,421.52 to 24,315.00.
In other financial markets, the initial knee-jerk reaction to the U.S. midterm election results faded a bit.
[truncated]

La realidad política paraguaya es bifronte y trágica. Desde la era democrática que arranca en 1989 confronta períodos de estabilidad con tiempos de escándalo, corrupción y violencia política. El presidente Santiago Peña, un “amigo de Estados Unidos e Israel”, fiel integrante del “Escudo de las Américas” también cayó en ese mismo abismo. El primero en caer fue el Presidente más votado, Raúl Cubas, en 1999, por causas políticas. El segundo, el ex obispo Fernando Lugo en 2010.
Pero el primer presidente civil de la democracia (1993-1998) fue llevado a la justicia y condenado a cuatro años de cárcel por prácticas corruptas, Juan Carlos Wasmosy. Su sucesor, Luis González Macchi recibió dos condenas por corrupción. En esos años, como ahora, miles de ahorristas fueron estafados. Colapsaron seis bancos mayoritarios debido a la combinación de créditos otorgados de manera irregular a personas vinculadas a los directores, operaciones de lavado de dinero, nula regulación bancaria y complicidad de funcionarios clave del Gobierno y el Banco Central. El desfalco se estimó inicialmente en más de 137 millones de dólares. De 40 bancos y 60 sobrevivieron menos de 14. Un eco del pasado en este presente.
Paraguay recuperó la credibilidad de los organismos financieros internacionales en julio de 2024, un año después de la llegada al poder de Santiago Peña. La calificadora Moody’s por primera vez le otorgó el grado de inversión al país. Luego la siguió S&P Global Ratings. El reconocimiento técnico por parte de los mercados internacionales fue reflejo de reformas institucionales, elogiada estabilidad macroeconómica y fortalecimiento fiscal. Quedaron atrás los fantasmas de crisis y cesaciones de pagos y sus miles de víctimas atrapadas en la timba financiera.
Pero, la pesadilla regresó de repente y en el momento menos pensado, mientras Peña, ex ministro de Hacienda de Horacio Cartes, un economista egresado de Columbia, se jactaba de haber conducido al país “al despertar de un gigante”. La decepción no tardó en llegar, a poco más de la mitad de su Gobierno de cinco años.
Todo empezó en octubre cuando el mandatario y su vicepresidente, Pedro Alliana, deciden formar carpa aparte de su padrino político, el acaudalado empresario tabacalero Cartes, devenido a político un año antes de ser elegido Presidente en 2013. Ambos no aceptaron que Cartes, presidente del partido Colorado oficialista, les imponga el candidato a Vicepresidente para las elecciones de 2028.
Las primarias están programadas para julio de 2027. “No se debe confundir lealtad con obsecuencia”, dijo Alliana. “Yo voy a elegir al que me va a acompañar en la chapa presidencial”, desafió. Alliana dejó abierta la posibilidad de competir por fuera del movimiento cartista y se retrató con los gobernadores de los 15 departamentos más importantes del país y con parlamentarios disidentes del cartismo. La prensa lo identificó como el nacimiento del Peñismo, partidarios de Santiago Peña.
La inestabilidad política y bancaria
Pero Cartes fue el que hizo detonar la bomba. “Ordená el problema de tu banquito”, se le escuchó decir, dirigiéndose al Presidente. A través de sus partidarios en el Senado hizo pedir un informe al Banco Central sobre la situación del Ueno Bank, una entidad que cobró un crecimiento vertiginoso desde que Peña asumió el poder en 2023. Como se sabe, el BCP lo intervino este 3 de noviembre. Su índice de solvencia se desplomó y cerca de 3 millones de personas quedaron sin la posibilidad de acceder a sus activos.
Había un trasfondo grave. En marzo de 2019, Peña compró acciones de la financiera Credicentro de la familia Vázquez que pasó a llamarse Ueno Holding. A marzo de 2025 contaba con 6.144 millones de guaraníes (poco más de un millón de dólares). Cuando se supo, dijo que vendió sus acciones y acusó a la prensa de falsear la verdad. “Nunca fui parte de Ueno Bank”, dijo.
