Die Islamische Republik leidet infolge des von den USA und Israel Ende Februar begonnenen Kriegs unter einem verstärkten Erdgasmangel. Nach Angaben aus Teheran wurden Gasanlagen vor allem im Süden des Landes von US-Angriffen getroffen, Raffinerien fielen aus. Ende Oktober riefen die Behörden die Menschen in Iran zu Einsparungen beim Gasverbrauch auf.
Resaei sagte den Angaben zufolge weiter, Putin habe bei dem Treffen mit Blick auf die Golfregion »die Notwendigkeit regionaler Sicherheitsmechanismen« und »die Unzulässigkeit jeglicher Einmischung von äußeren Kräften« betont. Anfang Oktober hatte Putin seinem iranischen Kollegen Masoud Pezeshkian laut Medienberichten zugesichert, »alles« zu tun, um zu einem Ende des Kriegs in der Golfregion beizutragen.
Iran meldet Brände auf fünf Tankern und einem Schlepper in der Straße von Hormus
In der Straße von Hormus sind nach iranischen Angaben derweil fünf Öltanker und ein Schlepper in Brand geraten. Die Revolutionswächter berichteten am Donnerstag von zwei betroffenen Tankern und einem Schlepper, die iranische Armee meldete drei weitere Tanker, die auf Seeminen gefahren seien. Eine unabhängige Bestätigung der Vorfälle durch Schifffahrtsbehörden lag zunächst nicht vor:
- Ein großer Öltanker sei in der Nacht auf eine Mine gefahren und habe Feuer gefangen, erklärten die Revolutionswächter laut der Nachrichtenagentur Fars. Das Schiff habe versucht, eine »illegale Passage südlich der Straße von Hormus« zu durchqueren.
- Ein Schlepper, der sich dem zweiten Tanker zum Löschen genähert habe, sei ebenfalls in Brand geraten.
- Ein weiterer Tanker sei beim Verlassen des östlichen Teils der Meerenge durch einen Großbrand zum Stillstand gekommen.
- Später meldete die iranische Armee drei weitere Zwischenfälle. Am frühen Morgen sei ein Öltanker östlich der Meerenge auf eine Seemine gefahren.
- Gegen Mittag hätten in den dortigen Gewässern zwei weitere Tanker Minen getroffen und Feuer gefangen, berichtete die amtliche Nachrichtenagentur Irna.
Die britische Überwachungsstelle UKMTO meldete unterdessen einen Angriff auf einen Tanker rund 90 Kilometer vor der Nordküste Katars. Das Schiff sei von zwei nicht identifizierten Geschossen getroffen worden. Zu Schäden oder möglichen Opfern machte UKMTO keine Angaben. Der Angriffsort liegt etwa 500 Kilometer westlich der Straße von Hormus.
Die Nachrichtenagentur Fars berichtete außerdem, die Einheit für elektronische Kriegsführung der Marine der Revolutionswächter habe zwei Drohnen des in den USA entwickelten Typs Lucas unter ihre Kontrolle gebracht.
Seit Beginn des Irankriegs Ende Februar hat Teheran die für den weltweiten Handel mit Öl und Gas wichtige Meerenge weitgehend blockiert. Durch die für den weltweiten Ölhandel wichtige Wasserstraße wird normalerweise etwa ein Fünftel des weltweiten Ölverbrauchs transportiert. Iran greift dort regelmäßig Schiffe an, denen er eine Durchfahrt ohne seine Genehmigung vorwirft.
Die USA haben als Reaktion darauf eine Seeblockade iranischer Häfen verhängt und unterstützen Schiffe bei der Durchfahrt durch die Meerenge.
Das US-Militär erklärte im vergangenen Monat, es habe den Golfstaaten seit dem Sommer geholfen, 1,5 Milliarden Barrel Öl durch die Straße von Hormus zu exportieren.

European shares tumbled on Friday as global investors grappled with uncertainty over AI stocks, following the Democrats’ sweeping victory in the US midterm elections. The drop is partly due to fears that Democrats could curb the development of AI data centres, which are widely unpopular among US voters. Follow our liveblog for all the latest updates.
Races in Alaska, Mississippi to determine strength of Democratic majority
Democrats could still add Senate seats, as Alaska and Mississippi are undecided.
Trump blames Democrats winning midterms for US stocks fall
US President Donald Trump attributed Thursday's stock market freefall to the electoral victory of his rival Democratic Party in midterm elections earlier this week.
"The Stock Market crashed today because the Dumocrats had a big Tuesday - So sad to see, you only have yourselves to blame!" Trump posted on his Truth Social platform after US markets closed for the day.
Analysts attributed Thursday's stock selloff to fears of Democrats threatening the AI data centre investment boom, with the tech-focused Nasdaq suffering its worst session percentage-wise since April 2025.
🎥 'Like a cancer': How data centres became a key issue at midterms
Data centre regulation itself was not on most midterm ballots, and it wasn't among the top issues for most voters. But hardline stances against the server warehouses were woven into the platforms of many candidates, including the Democrats who upended longtime Republican control of the governorships in Texas, Ohio, Georgia, Nevada and Iowa --many of which are data centre hotspots.
European shares set to fall as global AI rout gathers pace
European shares were set to open lower on Friday amid a global market rout, capping a painful week as investors grappled with uncertainty over AI stocks after Democrats took control of US Congress.
Futures tied to the EURO STOXX 50 Index were down 1 percent at 6:52 GMT, with contracts tracking benchmarks in Germany and the UK down 0.8 percent and 0.9 percent, respectively.
Fears that a Democrat-led Congress could seek curbs on AI data-centre spending added to concerns over weak returns, lofty valuations and debt-fueled investment.
Hello and welcome to our liveblog where we bring you the latest as the final US midterm votes are counted.
European shares fell on Friday, with losses across the board as a global market rout gathered steam, capping a painful week as investors grappled with uncertainty over AI stocks after Democrats took control of the US Congress.

"If you start to see stock portfolios hit, that is going to act as a real drag on consumer sentiment," Streeter said, adding that she expects market volatility to persist till at least January when there could be more clarity on the Democrats' approach to AI policy.

A202.text:
Tech stocks plunge as US midterm results fuel fears of tighter AI rules
Asian tech stocks fell sharply on Friday, driven by fears of tighter AI regulation following Democrats’ US midterm election victory. US voters widely oppose Data centres, and many winning candidates pledged to curb their development.
Asian tech firms suffered a bloodbath Friday as investors tracked a collapse on Wall Street fuelled by fears that Democrats will ramp up regulations of the AI industry following their blowout victory in this week's US midterm elections.
Read moreData centres on the ballot: Could AI infrastructure shape the US midterms?
Trading boards were a sea of red in early business, with Seoul and Tokyo taking the brunt of the selling as traders fled to the hills amid uncertainty about a sector that had pushed stock markets to record highs just five months ago.
While the historic "blue wave" in Tuesday's vote had been initially welcomed on hopes it could put pressure on President Donald Trump to wind down his war against Iran, fears about the impact on the AI buildout soon came to the fore.
Data centres have faced broad opposition from US voters across the political spectrum, and many midterm winners have pledged to put the brakes on such projects.
Analysts said investors were also spooked by a call from progressive US Senator Bernie Sanders for a national moratorium on their building.
The results compounded already heightened fears about the hundreds of billions firms had pumped into the sector and when they would see a return, while the recent spike in borrowing costs also fuelled concerns about their financial position.
The eye-watering rally in many companies' valuations had also caused unease on trading floors.
Michael Hewson at MCH Market Insights said investors were selling up because of "concerns that we might see greater opposition to AI buildout plans, with the results in Texas prompting concerns that politicians in the state might target Elon Musk's Tesla and SpaceX due to his support for Trump".
New York's Nasdaq plunged 5.5 percent in its worst day – percentage-wise – since April last year when Trump unveiled his wide-ranging global tariffs. The S&P 500 tanked more than four percent and the Dow more than three percent.
Read moreUS midterms: 'Donald Trump's wings have been more than clipped'
Bloomberg said the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index had collapsed around 16 percent this week, putting it on course for its worst run since April last year.
Trump blamed the collapse on the Democrats, writing on Truth Social: "The Stock Market crashed today because the Dumocrats had a big Tuesday - So sad to see, you only have yourselves to blame! President DONALD J. TRUMP."
The heavy selling continued in Asia.
Seoul plunged almost nine percent at one point, with chip giant SK hynix off 10 percent while rival Samsung was eight percent down.
The Kospi more than doubled between the end of December and mid-June, when it hit a record, and has since then lost almost 50 percent.
Tokyo dived seven percent as Kioxia and SoftBank gave back more than 10 percent, with Advantest more than eight percent lower.
TSMC's seven-percent drop dragged Taipei's Taiex around eight percent lower.
Hong Kong, Shanghai, Sydney and Singapore were all down more than one percent, with Wellington and Manila also in the red.
"The blood is in the streets, folks," said Neil Wilson at Saxo Markets.
"The fear is a total momentum unwind as Democrats pace the frontier and kibosh data centre buildout ... this looks totally overdone but the nature of sell-everything of this market means we need to look for some stability first."
The mood was also dampened by a fresh lift in oil prices, extending Thursday's gains after plunging on the midterm results amid hopes for an end to the Iran war.
Traders were keeping eyes on developments in the crisis after US and Iranian leaders had indicated progress earlier in the week.
[truncated]

A212.text:
Paraguay's president Pena impeached after resigning over banking scandal
Paraguay’s lower house voted unanimously to impeach President Santiago Pena on Thursday, just minutes after he announced his resignation on X. Protesters have rallied in the streets since the takeover of a bank linked to Pena blocked millions of people, including pensioners, from accessing their money.
Paraguayan President Santiago Pena will face an impeachment trial after a financial crisis that led the US-allied leader to resign Thursday, after a banking takeover blocked almost half the population from accessing their money.
Congress put Pena's resignation on hold while the impeachment process move forwards, which means he will remain in office provisionally.
The Central Bank's seizure of Pena-linked Ueno Bank two days earlier froze the deposits of some three million people, including pensioners, and sparked angry demonstrations across the country.
Thousands of Paraguayans gathered outside Congress on Thursday to protest against the president, who is still technically in power as his resignation awaits legislative approval.
"Give back the money," AFP journalists heard them yelling. Earlier demonstrations featured clashes with the police, who used tear gas and water cannons on the crowd.
"My family ran out of money, we don't have any cash. Santi (Pena) is a criminal, he has to go to jail," 21-year-old student protester Andres Maldonado said.
Lawmakers voted unanimously Thursday to launch impeachment proceedings against Pena over the crisis, alleging misconduct and a conflict of interest in dealings with the bank to which he is tied.
The right-wing president said he would attend his impeachment trial, which is set to begin Friday, after earlier apologising to the people of Paraguay.
"It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me," he said in a video posted on X announcing his resignation.
Pena's priority, he added, is "the peace of mind of Paraguayans who entrusted their savings to our financial system".
Pena's Interior Minister Enrique Riera also resigned from his post Thursday, according to a decree published in local media, with Carlos Benitez appointed to replace him in the interim.
Read moreParaguay, a tax and political haven for Brazil's far right
'Nowhere to live'
Paraguay's Central Bank said it took over Ueno due to a severe capital shortfall, in order to "protect depositors and preserve the stability of the financial system".
"Ueno approved a loan for us to buy our first house. But the funds were never disbursed, and now we have nowhere to live," 26-year-old Nadia Gonzalez, a mother of three, told AFP.
Long lines of people trying to withdraw their money from Ueno branches snaked down Asuncion's streets on Tuesday and Wednesday.
Pena owned shares in a group that controlled the bank, but he sold them last year.
He had attempted to ease tensions by requesting the resignation of Central Bank president Carlos Carvallo, who consented, and setting a five-day limit for the return of funds. Neither measure proved sufficient.
Congress called an extraordinary session of both chambers Thursday to decide whether to accept Pena's resignation or reject it and proceed with the impeachment process.
But the session failed to reach a quorum, so the vote did not go ahead.
A later extraordinary session scheduled the impeachment trial to begin on Friday morning.
"A criminal scheme has been set up here that has dedicated itself to draining a bank, under the protection of institutions he controlled as president of the republic," opposition lawmaker Raul Benitez stated.
The aim is to conclude the trial on Friday as a way to "reassure the public", ruling party Senator Derlis Maidana told reporters.
Vice President Pedro Alliana is set to take over as leader of the South American nation.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

A222.text:
Benjamin Netanyahu’s main rival secured nods on Thursday from a majority of lawmakers to try to form a government, but Israel’s president said it was still unclear who could break the election deadlock as he pledged to nominate a candidate on Sunday.
Israel’s Oct. 27 national ballot ended with no clear winner. Neither Prime Minister Netanyahu nor Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief, secured a clear path to a majority in parliament.
That has set up a tough task for President Isaac Herzog, whose mostly ceremonial role comes with the postelection responsibility of picking a candidate he believes has the best chance to form a coalition in a deeply divided country.
Four takeaways from Israel’s deadlocked election
Herzog held marathon talks with elected factions on Wednesday and Thursday, during which 67 of parliament’s 120 elected lawmakers endorsed Eisenkot, while 46 endorsed Netanyahu.
In televised remarks at the end of the talks, Herzog said that while the “results of the consultations may appear clear,” there were “mutual vetoes between the blocs and within the blocs themselves” that make it difficult to say who has the best shot to form a government.
Herzog said he would make a pick on Sunday, and that he would hold “personal talks with some of the party leaders” over the Israeli weekend, which runs Friday-Saturday.
Opinion: For Israel to change, Arab parties must be included
Once nominated by Herzog, the candidate will have 28 days to try to forge a government, with a possible 14-day extension.
Netanyahu will remain prime minister in a caretaker government until a new coalition is formed, or through another election which must be held if no candidate succeeds.
Netanyahu’s Likud won the most seats of any single party with 27 in the 120-seat Knesset, but Netanyahu’s wider religious-nationalist coalition garnered only 53 in total.
That was still better than Eisenkot’s anti-Netanyahu coalition spanning four centre-left to right-wing Jewish-led parties, which won just 48 seats despite pre-election polls pointing to a close race. Two parties representing Israel’s Arab minority won an unprecedented 19 seats.
In a setback for the prime minister on Thursday, United Torah Judaism, one of two major parties representing ultra-Orthodox Jewish voters and a long-standing Netanyahu coalition ally, declined to recommend any candidate to form a government during talks with Herzog.
And while Eisenkot, like Netanyahu, has so far ruled out forming a government with Israel’s two Arab-led parties, both factions endorsed Eisenkot, giving him backing from a comfortable majority of lawmakers.
Opinion: Israel finds itself at a crucial turning point
Netanyahu, at risk of losing power, has seized on an investigation by election officials into possible vote tampering to cast doubt on the results, accusing Arab-led parties of stealing the vote. Critics accuse Netanyahu and his partners of trying to undermine the results, which he denies.
Israel’s Central Election Committee said on Wednesday that the election’s integrity had not been compromised. The head of the committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, has called on Israel’s elected officials to protect public trust, rather than shake it.
“This is a real danger. One of the foundations of democracy is the peaceful transfer of power,” Sohlberg told Herzog at his residence on Wednesday. High voter turnout, including among the Arab minority, was a blessing, he said.
Netanyahu’s allies on the far-right, including National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, have called for the immediate arrest and interrogation of Arab party leaders.

A228.text:
Russian President Vladimir Putin’s envoy appeared with first lady Melania Trump at the White House on Thursday as she brought together Russian and Ukrainian officials to mark the localized ceasefire she brokered between their nations.
Speaking at the invitation of the first lady, Kirill Dmitriev thanked Trump for her “distinguished humanitarian role” in securing the ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine. President Donald Trump did not appear.
Dmitriev added that Putin personally gave instructions as part of the operation and sent his thanks to Melania Trump. The event included officials from Russia and Ukraine to honour the ceasefire, which was signed Oct. 23.
Humanitarian mission reaches Ukraine’s battered Oleshky as localized truce holds
The head of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s party, Davyd Arakhamia, and Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, also spoke at the event.
Trump said that she hoped the suspension of hostilities in the ravaged, Russian-occupied Ukrainian village of Oleshky can lead to something more enduring than the six day ceasefire.
“What matters is not the modesty of this beginning but the determination to turn into something extraordinary,” she said.
The White House announced Oct. 23 that the first lady had brokered a ceasefire in the ravaged, Russian-occupied Ukrainian village of Oleshky so that humanitarian aid can be delivered and civilians can be evacuated from a place she said was “on the brink of disaster.”
The announcement came after Ukrainian, Russian and U.S. negotiators had reached an agreement to deliver relief to Oleshky in the war-divided region of Kherson in southern Ukraine.
The local ceasefire was in effect from Oct. 27 to Nov. 1 and amounted to the most significant truce since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine 4½ years ago.
Opinion: The crisis in Oleshky shows what a Russian victory in Ukraine would look like
An estimated 2,000 people remained in Oleshky when the temporary truce took hold on Oct. 27, lasting for six days before ending on Nov. 1. They were offered the choice of evacuating to territory controlled by Ukraine or Russia, or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies.
During the pause in hostilities, residents of Oleshky crossed into Ukrainian-held territory in a major evacuation operation. Evacuees wrapped in blue and yellow Ukrainian flags stepped off buses at the Ukrainian-Belarusian border and reunited with family members.
Ukrainian authorities have not said how many residents were evacuated from Oleshky and have restricted details of their route to protect those who remained and safeguard future humanitarian missions. Melania Trump said on social media that the humanitarian convoy could safely evacuate more than 750 people.

A230.text:
Corruption topped the list of concerns for voters who ousted Republicans and handed Democrats control of Congress in the midterm elections. Now, the newly empowered Democratic Party is putting the issue front and centre as its leaders chart their course for investigations and policymaking.
Senior Democrats in both chambers of Congress have vowed to marshal the subpoena powers and larger investigative staffs that come with their soon-to-be majorities to probe what they say is the self-enrichment that President Donald Trump and people in his orbit have done at the public’s expense. The Republican president and his White House have long denied any wrongdoing.
House Democrats are preparing a vast oversight agenda to look at how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office – and Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who’s in line to become House speaker, has not ruled out trying to impeach Trump for a third time.
Swing voters, economic worries drive decisive blue wave in U.S. midterms
Months ago, Jeffries tasked the ranking Democrats on the Oversight and Judiciary committees, Rep. Robert Garcia of California and Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, with leading the effort, as Democrats work to link the costs of public corruption to the affordability concerns hitting Americans’ pocketbooks.
“Lawyer up,” Garcia posted on X as election results favouring Democrats began coming in on Tuesday night.
The Senate is expected to conduct similar investigations.
“Americans want us to clean up corruption in government,” said Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., who is poised to return as Senate majority leader next year. “No American should have to make tradeoffs at the supermarket while Trump is making inside trades on the stock market.”
Investigation targets could include ICE raids, Epstein and DOGE
Garcia, the top Democrat on the Oversight and Government Reform Committee, has outlined five priorities, including Trump family business dealings, the administration’s handling of the Jeffrey Epstein investigation and Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations. Rep. Jared Huffman of California, the ranking Democrat on the Natural Resources Committee, said he wants to dig into Trump’s White House ballroom and other construction projects, as well as the Trump family’s role in mineral deals.
With the House majority comes an infusion of congressional committee staff and resources, and the effort is expected to be sprawling, involving House committees with authority to conduct oversight on Cabinet officials and the agencies they lead.
In the Senate, Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., who is expected to become the chairman of the Homeland Security Committee’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, said his panel will want to look into Trump’s real estate projects around the nation’s capital and his crypto dealings with special envoy Steve Witkoff. Witkoff is a longtime ally who partnered with Trump on the president’s family cryptocurrency venture, World Liberty Financial.
Six takeaways from Democrats’ resounding midterm sweep
“The tentacles of corruption reach deep in this administration, and they have added costs to everyday Americans,” Blumenthal said in an interview with The Associated Press on Wednesday. The senator added that he also wants hearings on ICE raids, the actions of the Department of Government Efficiency and Medicare plans he says are too restrictive and have cost some patients care.
Meanwhile, Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon, who is in line to become Senate Finance Committee chairman, ticked off several investigative targets that he describes as part of an “accountability” agenda, including banks that he contends ignored red flags about the financial dealings of Epstein and pharmaceutical companies that have profited from their ties to the Trump administration.

A233.text:
With the U.S. midterms over, Democrats are turning to what could become one of their most crowded and unpredictable presidential primaries in decades, a 2028 contest likely to expose the party’s divide over how to win back the White House.
No Democrat has emerged as a clear favourite in a field that could attract dozens of contenders, while Republicans have a smaller group of widely discussed candidates, led by Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, to succeed President Donald Trump, who is constitutionally barred from seeking a third term.
Potential Democratic candidates, including sitting governors and senators, have spent months cultivating donors, visiting states with early nominating contests and raising their national profiles, positioning themselves for a race that strategists expect to begin in earnest now that the midterms are over.
The sweeping victories by Democrats on Tuesday, when voters delivered a sharp rebuke to Trump and his agenda, will intensify discussions within both parties about how to win over an electorate unhappy with the country’s direction.
Swing voters, economic worries drive decisive blue wave in U.S. midterms
Despite their resounding victories on Tuesday, Democrats enter the 2028 campaign still divided over whether to tack to the centre or move further left on issues ranging from health care and taxes to policing and foreign policy.
Republican candidates will face a different challenge – how to distance themselves from Trump after Tuesday’s repudiation of his policies. They need to broaden their appeal beyond the president’s base while avoiding a break with the populist Make America Great Again movement that has come to define the party.
Trump, who has dominated the political landscape for a decade, may be reluctant to yield centre stage, and his continued influence with MAGA followers could complicate the path of the party’s next standard-bearer.
Looming Democratic battle
Doug Sosnik, a Democratic strategist, said both progressives and moderates will claim vindication in their ideological approaches, ensuring an intense internal battle over the party’s future as the 2028 race begins in earnest.
One of the most high-profile progressive wins came in the Michigan Senate contest, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed easily defeated Republican Mike Rogers in a likely 2028 presidential swing state, becoming the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate.
“All kinds of wings of the Democratic Party can find affirmation in the results last night,” Sosnik said on Wednesday. “I don’t think that anyone can, nor should they, try to contain the differences we have as a party.”
The party has not had a proper debate about its philosophy and direction since 2016, when Hillary Clinton won the nomination against a spirited challenge by U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders, a Vermont independent who describes himself as a democratic socialist, Sosnik said.
Several potential candidates have either acknowledged considering a White House run or declined to rule one out. Most spent the final weeks of the midterm campaign stumping for fellow Democrats in early nominating states such as Nevada, New Hampshire and South Carolina.
They include former Vice-President Kamala Harris, who lost to Trump in 2024, Governors Gavin Newsom of California and Andy Beshear of Kentucky, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, and U.S. Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, a leading progressive voice.
Reuters contacted representatives for nine of the party’s most prominent potential contenders. None confirmed a 2028 run.
Nine days after the Nov. 3 elections, several prospective Democratic candidates, including Buttigieg and another progressive, U.S. Representative Ro Khanna of California, are scheduled to attend a gathering in Denver hosted by Majority Democrats.

A304.text:
After cancer surgery, Pope Leo embarks on Latin America trip
ROME — Pope Leo XIV is kicking off a three-nation tour of Latin America with a visit to Uruguay, the region's least Catholic and most secular country, three weeks after undergoing lung cancer surgery that had put the entire trip into question.
Leo is due to arrive in Montevideo after a 13-and-a-half hour flight from Rome. He has a packed three-day itinerary in Uruguay including a visit to a neighborhood plagued by gang violence, a Mass in Paysandú, some 375 kilometers (230 miles) from the capital, and another Mass in the city of Florida, about 100 kilometers (60 miles) away.
The Uruguay leg is the first stop on what will be the longest and farthest trip of his pontificate, all being undertaken as the 71-year-old pope continues his recovery. The trip will also bring him to neighboring Argentina and finally back home to Peru, where Leo served as a missionary priest and bishop for two decades.
"His stamina is fantastic. The way that he's singing is incredible. And you can only sing if your lungs are really strong," said Maria Montserrat Alvar, the Vatican's new communications chief. She noted that Leo has passed the 14-day convalescence period required by doctors after his Oct. 13 surgery and is eager to get on the road.
"His doctors are very confident and he'll have plenty of medical care on board should something happen, but we don't see that in his prognosis or even in the way that he's acting," she said.
A first stop in secular Uruguay
In Uruguay, which hasn't had a papal visit since 1988, Leo is expected to try to remind the 3.5 million people of their strong Catholic heritage stemming from the times of Spanish colonial rule. He is likely to propose the faith anew as an answer to today's challenges and problems.
Upon arrival, Leo will meet with President Yamandú Orsi, leader of the center-left alliance that assumed power in Uruguay in March 2025, and then deliver his welcome address to government officials and diplomats. He finishes the long day with a vespers service at the city's cathedral.
Leo will find in Uruguay a country unlike any other in Latin America, which is home to around 40% of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics. Uruguay is considered the most secular country in the region, where only a fraction of people who identify as Catholic actually go to Mass regularly.
Uruguay was the first country in the world to legalize marijuana for recreational use, the second country in Latin America to decriminalize abortion, and the third country in the Americas to legalize same-sex marriage.
More recently, it became the first country in the region to approve assisted dying legislation over the strong opposition of the Catholic Church, evidence of Uruguay's entrenched, church-state separation that prohibits any mention of God in oaths of office.
Leo is expected to recall the church's opposition to abortion and euthanasia as part of his broader argument about upholding human dignity in all phases of life.
Uruguayan church officials have marveled at the apparent enthusiasm the visit has provoked, with reports that tickets to Leo's prayer vigil at Montevideo's Centenario Stadium were snapped up after two days.
"It seems that the pope's presence is shifting something here and is gradually breaking down this veil that has always sought to obscure and diminish the presence of the Catholic tradition that lies at the country's foundation," said Guzmán Carriquiry, the Uruguayan former head of the Vatican's pontifical commission for Latin America.
"I believe this pope will stir up questions in the hearts of Uruguayans -- disturbing questions -- questions about meaning and, we hope, questions about faith," he said.
Recalling the Catholic origins of independence
Carriquiry said he expects Leo will seek to revive the Catholic roots of Uruguay, especially when he travels to Florida on Sunday to mark an important Catholic feast day.

A305.text:
Paraguay's president is impeached minutes after resigning following a bank collapse
ASUNCIÓN, Paraguay — Paraguayan President Santiago Peña announced his resignation Thursday after the collapse of a major digital bank tied to his government triggered widespread protests, froze millions of people's savings and cost him the support of his own party.
The crisis at Ueno Bank turned Peña's long-ruling Colorado Party against him, a stunning reversal for the former International Monetary Fund economist who had enjoyed the backing of the country's most powerful politicians and was welcomed in Washington just weeks ago as a key ally of the Trump administration.
Minutes after Peña's announcement, the lower house voted 78-0 to impeach him, sending the charges to the Senate. Congressional leaders were expected to accept his resignation later Thursday, clearing the way for Vice President Pedro Alliana to be sworn in without waiting for a Senate trial.
Opposition senators were still demanding a trial, arguing that allowing Peña to resign would preserve his eligibility to become a senator for life, with legal protections that could prevent his prosecution.
As lawmakers debated his impeachment, Peña said in a video posted to X that he was stepping down in the interest of "the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions."
Even Peña's mentor, Colorado Party leader and former President Horacio Cartes, backed impeachment, saying the party would not side with "the plundering of public and private funds and pensioners' money." The United States Treasury sanctioned Cartes in 2023 over bribery allegations that the Trump administration lifted last year.
Peña, who until last year held a stake in a company linked to Ueno, expressed contrition. But he stopped short of accepting responsibility for the turmoil, which has left millions of depositors, retirees and workers scrambling to recoup their frozen savings and unpaid wages.
"I want to apologize to the people if I have failed them at any point," he said. "It was never my intention to betray the trust they placed in me."
The turmoil has hit Paraguay's currency. The guaraní fell nearly 4% against the U.S. dollar Thursday, bringing its losses this week to nearly 7%, according to central bank exchange-rate data.
From star lender to seized bank
Ueno Bank, which exploded from an obscure finance company to a household name in less than five years, claimed more than 60% of Paraguay's adults as customers. Many Paraguayans are left asking how a bank linked to the president could grow so rapidly in size and importance despite repeated warnings about its lending practices.
The answer lies in the uncomfortable proximity of Peña's Colorado Party to the country's regulators and business elite, a weakness that has endured even as steady economic management and rapid growth recently earned Paraguay coveted investment-grade credit ratings.
"Santiago Peña and the Colorado Party have stolen all our savings," said Luis Pineda, one of the protesters marching to Congress on Wednesday. "We are fed up with 70 years of plunder."
Soon after winning its banking license in 2023, Ueno seemed to be everywhere in Paraguay. The digital lender, a rebranded version of a decades-old finance company, lured customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries, grew to more than 70 locations, sponsored Paraguay's national soccer team and plastered its name on the country's main stadium.
Government money poured into Ueno's coffers under Peña. He also appointed Carlos Carvallo, president of Financiera Ueno, the predecessor to Ueno Bank, to run the central bank, the agency charged with supervising the digital lender.
As of last month, Ueno reported holding roughly $800 million in public deposits, about a quarter of its total, including money from the state pension and health fund and the operators of Paraguay's giant hydroelectric dams.

A37.text:
Tankers hit in Hormuz as Iran keeps up pressure after US vote
DUBAI, Nov 5 (Reuters) - Iran reported three more tankers had been damaged in the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, making clear that shipping would remain in peril as long as the war in the Gulf is unresolved, now that US voters have punished President Donald Trump for waging it.
The electoral rout that cost Trump's Republicans control of Congress has prompted a stark reassessment of the conflict's political cost in Washington, led by Vice President JD Vance, who said in a long social media post on Wednesday that the war was to blame for his party's defeat.
In a mocking reply on Thursday, Iran's Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, Vance's opposite number at previous peace talks, accused Vance of letting Trump double down like a "losing gambler" by planning more US strikes.
If Vance believed the war was a mistake he should persuade Trump to call it off, Qalibaf said: "Skip the TED talk. Why not say this to your boss?"
Oil prices have plunged in recent days as traders wagered that Trump, chastened by voters, may be less likely to restart the strikes he launched alongside Israel as "Operation Epic Fury" in February. Prices bounced back slightly on Thursday but are down more than $20 a barrel from last week.
Iranian officials have been meeting with Qatari mediators since last week to discuss proposals to end the hostilities. But neither side has announced any breakthroughs on the major issues that have prevented any peace agreement so far.
ATTACKS ON TANKERS AT RECORD PACE
Meanwhile, attacks on tankers in the Gulf are still running close to a record pace. At least five vessels have reported incidents since Sunday, according to UK maritime security agency UKMTO, around the same rate as in October when the agency said 35 vessels were hit, the most of any month of the war.
The UKMTO reported that a vessel had been struck by two unidentified projectiles late on Wednesday.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards, who do not typically acknowledge firing on merchant ships but say the transit route is unsafe without Tehran's consent, said two tankers had struck naval mines and another had caught fire on Thursday.
On Wednesday Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei said there should not be "even the slightest inclination towards submission" to the United States, which he said would remain hostile towards Iran no matter which party was in power.
'HE IS PLANNING TO BOMB IRAN'
When asked about Vance's comments on the war on Wednesday, Trump defended the decision to launch it, saying it was important to prevent Iran from getting a nuclear weapon, a justification he has repeatedly cited.
A White House adviser told Reuters that some officials and staff inside the White House viewed Vance's post as a foreign policy break from the president and a public recognition of the war's economic consequences.
But two sources told Reuters they believed Trump was still likely to order resumed hostilities.
"He is planning to bomb Iran. Don’t listen to what he’s saying. He held off because of the midterms. We asked him to hold off until the midterms," said one of the sources. The other said Trump did not have anything to lose politically now that the midterms were over.
Peacemaking efforts have revolved around the future status of the strait, a US blockade on Iranian ports, sanctions on the Islamic Republic and a resumption of negotiations over Tehran's nuclear programme.
A senior Iranian official said this week that the two sides remain far apart.
Qatar said on Tuesday that the United States and Iran were committed to mediation efforts and were reviewing proposals aimed at bridging their differences, adding that there had been developments in talks with both sides.
(Reporting by Nerijus Adomaitis in Oslo and Reuters Iran newsroomWriting by Angus McDowallEditing by Peter Graff)

A505.text:
Kremlin accuses Europe of struggling to decide who will speak for it at future Ukraine security talks
MOSCOW, Nov 6 - The Kremlin accused Europe on Friday of struggling to decide who would represent it in any future talks about ensuring the continent's security as part of a potential Ukraine settlement.
The United States, Ukraine, NATO and European partners recently held a meeting in Brussels regarding security guarantees for Ukraine and a broader European security architecture, while US President Donald Trump spoke on Thursday about "a big agreement" that "might involve all of Europe."

A524.text:
Pope Leo starts South America ‘homecoming’ tour a month after lung surgery
ABOARD THE PAPAL FLIGHT, Nov 6 - Pope Leo left on Friday for an ambitious 12-day trip across South America expected to attract millions-strong crowds, as the first US-born pope returns to a Catholic stronghold where he lived for decades as a missionary.
Leo, who is 71 and underwent lung cancer surgery last month, will visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru through November 17 on one of the most demanding overseas tours taken by a Catholic leader in decades.
The Vatican said this week that the pope had completely healed from his operation and no special precautions were being taken for the tour, on which Leo will travel some 31,000 km (19,300 miles) across 10 cities and give 36 speeches.
The pope, who was born in Chicago but spent decades in Peru and became a Peruvian citizen, considers the tour a "homecoming to places where he spent a long time and to which he feels closely connected," said Vatican spokesperson Matteo Bruni.
Leo told pilgrims at his weekly audience in St. Peter's Square on Wednesday that during the trip he was hoping to "strengthen the faith, renew hope, (and) rekindle the fire of charity".
POPE EXPECTED TO ADDRESS REGIONAL INSTABILITY
The pope, who departed from Rome's Fiumicino airport early on Friday morning, is due to arrive in Uruguay at 4:30 p.m. (1930 GMT). He will stay in the country until Sunday, visiting three cities before continuing on for three days in Argentina and six days in Peru.
Leo, who has forcefully decried the direction of global leadership in recent months, will address the governments in each country in closely watched speeches. He will also lead outdoor Masses at major local sites, visit a prison in Argentina and head to remote Andean communities in Peru by helicopter.
On Sunday, Leo will give an address to Argentine President Javier Milei, a right-wing libertarian seen as a close ally to US President Donald Trump, who lambasted Leo earlier this year after the pope criticized the Iran war.
Bruni said the pope's speeches during the tour would address a range of issues facing the continent, including environmental destruction, arms trafficking and regional political instability.
"The pope brings a message of communion and unity, an invitation to recognise one another ... as members of one same family," he said.
The late Pope Francis, who was Leo's predecessor and from Argentina, visited Peru in 2018 but never returned home. A pope has not visited Argentina or Uruguay since the late 1980s.
Argentine officials have said some 7 million people will attend events with Leo.
VATICAN NOT TAKING ADDITIONAL MEDICAL PRECAUTIONS
Latin America has long been the world's largest Catholic region in absolute numbers, but the Church has been losing ground recently to fast-growing evangelical denominations and has struggled to respond to progressive social attitudes and individualized forms of worship.
Local Catholic leaders hope Leo's visit can reenergize the faith across the region and also help repair the Church's standing after abuse scandals have tarnished its reputation.
Leo will hold several meetings with survivors of sexual abuse by Catholic clergy during the trip, the Vatican has said, without yet providing further details.
The pope was treated in October for lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer. His doctors have said the disease was localized and he would not require any further treatments.
Bruni said Leo had recovered enough that no additional medical measures would be necessary during his trip.
Medical experts told Reuters the decision by Leo's doctors to clear him to fly should indicate the risk of complications from his surgery was low, that his operated lung had fully expanded and any surgical wounds were healing without signs of infection.

A525.text:
Putin seizes control of Japan Tobacco’s Russian assets
- Putin signed a decree to temporarily seize Japan Tobacco International’s Russian assets. Industrial Assets will manage four JTI businesses, and Tokyo protested through diplomatic channels.
- The Russian business is a major part of Japan Tobacco, bringing about 10% of revenue and 25% of operating profit. Shares in Japan Tobacco fell in Tokyo after the news.
- The move deepens tensions between Japan and Russia after sanctions over Ukraine. Russia has also taken control of other foreign firms, and Japan has sent officials to protect company assets.
AI generated
MOSCOW/TOKYO – Russian President Vladimir Putin has signed a degree to temporarily seize the Russian assets of Japan Tobacco International (JTI), making it the latest foreign company to lose control of local operations in a widening crackdown.
The move drew an immediate rebuke from Tokyo on Nov 6, whose already sour relations with Moscow have deteriorated sharply in recent months.
Stakes in four businesses of JTI, which is part of Japan Tobacco (JT) and is Russia’s biggest tobacco manufacturer, will now be under the administration of Russian company Industrial Assets, according to the decree signed on Nov 5.
The Japanese government owns around 37% of shares in Japan Tobacco, whose brands include Winston and Camel cigarettes. Those shares were set to fall by the daily allowable limit in Tokyo on Nov 6 with no shares changing hands due to a glut of sell orders.
“The Japanese government has consistently urged Russia to ensure that the interests of Japanese citizens and companies are not harmed,” Japanese Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama told a regular press conference on Nov 6.
“We have already protested through diplomatic channels and requested that the measure be withdrawn.”
The decree gave no reason for the seizure, but the Kremlin has linked similar moves in the past to the behaviour of countries it designates as “hostile”.
In an emailed statement, JTI said it was aware of the decree and was “assessing the situation and our options, prioritising our stakeholders, most notably our employees”.
The Russian business accounts for about 10% of JT Group’s revenue and roughly 25% of its operating profit.
Strained relations
The decree follows Russia’s decision to place the assets of Swiss food giant Nestle, German wholesaler Metro AG and French retailer Auchan under temporary management in September.
Moscow took control of the Russian assets of four more European companies in October, citing those nations’ support for Ukraine and what it called illegal expropriations of Russian property.
Relations between Japan and Russia have been strained since Tokyo and other capitals slapped broad sanctions on Moscow after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
But they have spiralled in recent months, following Putin’s visit to a disputed island close to Japan in August and the detention of Japanese journalist in the far eastern Russian region of Sakhalin on suspicion of espionage.
Russia’s foreign ministry in October also said it considered a drone sale to Ukraine by a Japanese company to be a hostile step and warned of a harsh response.
Until at least 2025, most Japanese companies that remained in Russia had been hunkering down, hoping for business conditions to improve.
Around three quarters of 50 companies surveyed by Japanese trade promotion agency JETRO in September 2025 said they planned to maintain the status quo over the next one to two years, and only 6% said they would scale back, relocate or withdraw.
Japan sent several officials to Moscow earlier in 2026 to facilitate communication and help protect assets owned by Japanese companies operating there, its trade ministry said. REUTERS

A527.text:
Pope Leo on emotional South America tour weeks after cancer surgery
- Pope Leo XIV begins a 12-day South America tour on Nov 6, three weeks after lung cancer surgery, aiming to renew faith, hope and charity.
- He will visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, meeting leaders, prisoners and the poor, with major security in Uruguay and strong public interest across the region.
- The trip is deeply personal, especially in Peru and Argentina, where his priesthood and Pope Francis’s legacy add symbolism, emotion and expectations of pastoral support.
AI generated
VATICAN CITY – Pope Leo XIV heads to South America on Nov 6 for an emotionally charged reunion with the continent that helped shape his priesthood, three weeks after undergoing lung cancer surgery.
The 71-year-old head of the Catholic Church will in 12 days visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru in one of the most intense papal foreign trips in decades, meeting political leaders, prisoners, the poor, as well as old friends.
The Church’s first US-born pope served for almost two decades in Peru as a missionary, forming a deep attachment to the continent.
Leo said on Nov 4 that he was looking forward to returning to those countries “so dear to me”.
The head of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics said he hoped the trip would “strengthen faith, renew hope, (and) rekindle the fire of charity” in the countries, which share challenges from rising inequality and violence, to demographic falls and the decline of Catholicism.
Despite undergoing an operation on Oct 13 to remove a cancerous tumour, doctors have given him the all-clear to travel, and the Vatican said no special medical measures were necessary beyond the standard care on papal trips.
Secular Uruguay
Leo begins his trip in Uruguay, Latin America’s most secular country – and one of the wealthiest – where a tight security operation is in place, with some 5,000 police officers and 1,000 soldiers mobilised.
He will be driven along Montevideo’s waterfront promenade in a custom-made popemobile, before meeting left-wing Uruguayan President Yamandu Orsi and receiving the keys to the city.
“I have family members who plan to go to the waterfront to watch him pass,” Janet Rodriguez, 47, told AFP.
“I won’t be going, as I’m not religious. But it’s great that someone of such importance is coming,” she said.
Cardinal Daniel Sturla, archbishop of Montevideo, told AFP there was “widespread interest in the pope’s visit that goes well beyond the confines of the Catholic Church”, with tickets for masses in Paysandu and Florida quickly running out.
The liberal nation is at odds with the centuries-old institution on same-sex marriage, abortion and euthanasia – which was legalised last year – and Leo is expected to appeal to protect life as well as traditional family values.
Uruguay has the highest suicide rate in Latin America and the pope may talk about mental health, particularly when visiting the Casavalle neighbourhood in Montevideo, notorious for high levels of poverty and extreme violence.
‘Symbolism and emotion’
The Pope will travel on Nov 8 to Argentina, the homeland of his predecessor Pope Francis, who disappointed many Argentinians by not returning to visit during his papacy.
Leo’s trip is seen as a double homecoming of sorts, US-based Vatican expert Christopher White told AFP.
“History’s first Latin American pope, Francis, never returned to his homeland. Leo, a Peruvian citizen, now carries forward that mantle and legacy,” said White, author of a book on Pope Leo.
The South America trip culminates in Peru, and Leo’s arrival there on Nov 4 will be “a moment full of symbolism and emotion”, he said.
The country has been gripped by pope fever.
In Lima, vendors are selling T-shirts and rosaries with his image on them, while Leo bread is on sale in bakeries. Inmates in a women’s prison are crafting dolls in his likeness.
A towering, 14m tall statue of Leo has also been erected in the port city of Callao, which he is to visit.

A545.text:
Trump says he met Putin envoy, sees Ukraine deal soon
- Trump said he met Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev and expects a Ukraine peace deal soon, with US-led talks due in Abu Dhabi from Nov 10 to 11.
- Melania Trump helped broker a six-day ceasefire in Oleshky and hosted Russian and Ukrainian officials, who praised her peace efforts and exchanged gifts.
- US officials are discussing security guarantees for Ukraine and Europe, while Democrats’ new Congress majority may press for more Ukraine aid and tougher scrutiny of Trump’s Russia stance.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump said he met privately on Nov 5 with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s envoy after the Russian official appeared with representatives from Ukraine at a White House event organised by US first lady Melania Trump.
Trump would not disclose what he discussed with Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev but predicted a deal could emerge soon aimed at resolving the Russian war in Ukraine.
A US delegation is scheduled to mediate talks in Abu Dhabi from Nov 10 to 11 between representatives from Russia and Ukraine.
Trump, speaking to reporters at the White House, said the war was close to being settled and that ending it might involve all of Europe.
“It’s going to be a big agreement, and it’s going to involve more than Ukraine... I could even say it might involve all of Europe. It’s going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone’s going to be thrilled,” Trump said.
Trump has frequently predicted an agreement to end Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II was close. However, negotiations have picked up in recent weeks.
Trump said he did not meet with the Ukrainian delegation on Nov 5.
Trump envoy Jared Kushner said US officials meeting in Brussels on Nov 5 held “productive and substantive discussions” with Ukraine, NATO and European partners on security guarantees for Ukraine and a broader European security architecture.
Kushner said in a social media post that negotiators were exploring five principal goals: Permanent security consultations, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, and an enduring framework for long-term European security and stability.
“Any arrangements must fully respect the sovereignty, territorial integrity, and independent decision-making of every nation,” Kushner said.
“Each country will retain authority over its own security and alliances, and no country would have a veto over another’s sovereign choices.
“NATO will remain central to European collective defence, and this initiative would build upon existing institutions and commitments.”
US First Lady brings two sides together
Dmitriev was among the officials at the rare face-to-face event with Ukrainian representatives at the White House to mark a six-day ceasefire that Melania Trump helped broker in the Russian-controlled city of Oleshky.
“We have chosen humanity over war,” the First Lady said at the event. “We must use the courage we brought to Oleshky to find common ground through a shared concern for the suffering of innocent people.”
Melania Trump said she was “involved in every stage of the planning” of the temporary ceasefire, including reviewing aerial images and assessing roadways and hospital access.
President Trump, who did not attend the event, has lauded his wife’s role in the Oleshky ceasefire, telling reporters in October that “she does better than our professionals”.
Ukrainian lawmaker David Arakhamia and Dmytro Lubinets, the country’s human rights ombudsman, also attended the event. They urged Slovenian-born Melania Trump to keep up her peace efforts.
Both sides presented the first lady with thank-you gifts.
Russia’s Dmitriev gave her a drawing of pink hearts from an Oleshky girl and said the child “chose to live with her family in Russia”, nodding to the fight over displaced Ukrainian children in Russia. “I love Melania,” the drawing read.

A550.text:
US watchdog calls for truth commission to investigate Church abuses cases in Peru
LIMA, Nov 5 - A US-based clergy abuse watchdog on Thursday called for the creation of a truth commission in Peru to investigate sexual abuse in the Catholic Church, on the eve of a visit by Pope Leo to South America where the Vatican says he will meet abuse survivors.
Anne Barrett Doyle, co-director of BishopAccountability.org, which tracks Catholic clergy abuse allegations worldwide, accused Peru's Church hierarchy of secrecy and of failing to adequately confront allegations of abuse.
"The stubborn secrecy of Peruvian Church leaders puts children at risk, deprives victims of validation, and prevents civil authorities from identifying and prosecuting the complicit," Barrett Doyle said at a press conference in Lima.
Representatives of the Archdiocese of Lima and the Peruvian Episcopal Conference, which represents the country's Catholic bishops, did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Peru's Church has faced a series of abuse scandals in recent years, most prominently involving Sodalitium Christianae Vitae, an ultraconservative Peru-founded Catholic group that expanded internationally. Pope Francis ordered the organization dissolved in 2025 after a Vatican investigation into allegations including sexual and psychological abuse.
Leo, the first US-born pope, will spend the final leg of his November 6-17 South American tour in Peru, the country where he arrived as a missionary in the 1980s, later became a citizen and served as bishop of Chiclayo. The Vatican has said he will meet with survivors of physical and sexual abuse during his visit to the region.
"Pope Leo has spoken compassionately about the need to accompany victims and to listen to them, but he has said almost nothing about holding bishops in his Church accountable. We hope we hear that message from him during this visit," Barrett Doyle said.
BishopAccountability.org on Thursday published a database identifying dozens of Peruvian clergy and religious figures it says have been accused of sexually abusing children or vulnerable people.
The group also called on Leo to condemn what it described as judicial persecution of journalists who have investigated abuse cases. REUTERS

A554.text:
Iran’s security chief discusses regional, bilateral affairs with Putin
MOSCOW, Nov 5 - Russian President Vladimir Putin met Iranian top security official Mohsen Rezaei at the Kremlin, Iran's state media reported on Thursday, after Iranian negotiators met with mediators to discuss proposals to end hostilities with the US.
Rezaei delivered a message from Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei to Putin, state media said. Putin's office also said the two met at the Kremlin.
"Important regional issues were discussed with Mr Putin, and significant conversations took place regarding the post-war period and regional security arrangements," Rezaei said after the meeting, referring to the war between Iran and the US.
Rezaei said the discussion also focused on the construction of a gas pipeline from Russia to Iran, aimed at addressing Iran's gas shortages and enabling Russia to sell its gas to Iran's neighbouring countries.
Khamenei said in a written statement on Wednesday there should not be "even the slightest inclination towards submission" to the United States.
Efforts for peace have been focused on the future status of the strategic Strait of Hormuz, a US blockade on Iranian ports, sanctions on the Islamic Republic and a resumption of negotiations over Tehran's nuclear programme.
A senior Iranian official said this week that the two sides remain far apart.
"However, we have told him [Putin] that on the issue of diplomacy, we have announced seven conditions to the Americans, as long as they do not execute our seven conditions we will neither open the Strait of Hormuz nor have negotiations," Rezaei added. REUTERS

A573.text:
US midterm elections 2026 live: Democrats exceed 250 House seats as blue wave sweeping Congress grows
Democrats widen gap in House chamber by flipping more seats, including in Ohio, Arizona and North Carolina; Ted Cruz calls election a ‘Watergate-level repudiation’
With the dust still settling on the midterms, attention is already turning to the Republicans who might seek to lead the party into the next presidential race in 2028. JD Vance, Ted Cruz and Ron DeSantis are among those in the mix, as the Republican party begins to reckon with the fallout from its midterms performance.
In this report, my colleague Ariana Baiolooks at the early jockeying, the potential contenders and what the midterm results could mean for the party’s future:
Welcome to our live coverage of the US midterm elections – here are some of the latest key developments.
A number of closely watched contests in the midterms are still to be called, including the final two US Senate races – in Mississippi and Alaska. The Democratic candidates are hoping to oust Republican incumbents to bolster their new majority in Congress. Right now, Democrats have a 106-seat majority as we await final results.
Democrats flipped another eight House seats, strengthening their majority in the lower chamber. Democrats are now leading Republicans 253 to 157, with 25 races left to call, as a number of GOP representatives felt the weight of the blue wave that has swept their party out of power. Republicans held on to two House seats in the west as congressman Mike Kennedy won re-election in Utah and Amanda McKinney won in Washington.
Democratic socialist Nithya Raman was elected to serve as the mayor of Los Angeles, eking out a narrow win over incumbent Karen Bass, in a major shake-up in local politics that reflects the growing dissatisfaction with the direction of the city. The progressive urban planner had served on LA’s city council since 2020.
Harmeet Dhillon, a key Trump ally, resigned from her position leading the justice department’s Civil Rights division. Attorney general Todd Blanche said he accepted her notice. Dhillon is the first high-ranking justice department official to leave after the midterm elections. Democrats are expected to use their power in taking control of Congress to aggressively investigate executive agencies, including the justice department.
Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic senator-elect in Michigan, said the new majority in the upper chamber needed “action” from their leader. On the campaign trail El-Sayed refused to back Senator Chuck Schumer, who currently serves as the minority leader. Speaking to CNN, El-Sayed reiterated that Senator Chris Van Hollen, the Maryland Democrat, would be an “amazing Senate majority leader”, but didn’t completely rule out supporting Schumer.
Joining the chorus of Republicans who blasted their party’s midterms performance is Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, who said the GOP were handed an “ass-kicking” in losing control of Congress. “It was not simply a bad 2006 midterm election, it was a Watergate-level repudiation,” he said on his podcast.
The Nasdaq share index had its worst day in 19 months after slumping 5.5% on Thursday amid growing signs the artificial intelligence industry will face tougher regulation because of the midterm results.
Donald Trump signed a proclamation that preserves the Oval Office and Cabinet Room as national monuments in his first official action after the Republican wipeout.

A574.text:
Gadi Eisenkot, the main rival to Benjamin Netanyahu, secured endorsements on Thursday from a majority of lawmakers to try to form a government but Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, said it was still unclear who could break the deadlock and that he would decide on Sunday which of the two men should try first.
Of the Knesset’s 120 elected lawmakers, 67 had endorsed Eisenkot through several days of talks with Herzog, while 46 endorsed Netanyahu. Herzog said on Thursday that while the “results of the consultations may appear clear”, there were “mutual vetoes between the blocs and within the blocs themselves” that make it difficult to say who has the best shot to form a government.
He said he would make a pick on Sunday, and that he would hold “personal talks with some of the party leaders” over the Israeli weekend, which runs Friday-Saturday.
A bitterly contested election last month, seen by many observers as one of the most consequential for Israel in many decades, ended with neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot, a former military general and chief of staff, securing a clear pathway to power.
Netanyahu’s coalition lost its majority, dropping from 68 to 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. The Change bloc of Zionist parties led by Eisenkot has 48 seats, leaving parties representing Israeli Palestinians as potential kingmakers with a record 19 seats. The Joint List has 11, while the more conservative, Islamist Ra’am has eight.
In Israel’s political system, the otherwise largely ceremonial president decides which candidate has the best initial chance of building a stable coalition to rule.
Both Arab-majority parties reported backing Eisenkot, according to Haaretz. United Torah Judaism, though often aligned with Netanyahu, did not endorse either man.
Turnout among Arab Israelis – Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, who constitute 20% of the population – more than doubled to about 80%, transforming the political landscape. Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and Gaza had no vote.
The leader of Israel’s main Palestinian coalition has admitted to “disagreements with Eisenkot on many issues” but said on Thursday that Palestinian voters wanted change after facing intensified racism, discrimination, crime and exclusion under the current coalition.
“We are not choosing between good and better but between what we see as bad and even worse,” Yousef Jabareen said, according to Israeli media.
Last month, Jabareen told the Guardian that the first demand of Arab Israeli voters was to get rid of the Netanyahu government, and in particular its most extreme members, Itamar Ben-Gvir, the national security minister, and Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister.
Eisenkot has also put conditions on any potential coalition with Arab parties: they have to recognise that Israel is a Jewish state, accept compulsory national service – either civil or military – and denounce Hamas as a terrorist organisation.
Jabareen and the Joint List have suggested they would support an opposition from the outside with tactical voting in the Knesset. Ra’am has said it would join a new government led by Eisenkot.
Herzog, who met delegations from the Palestinian Israeli parties and other small parties, has called on all to help avert another round of elections.
“Any reasonable person need only look at the security and diplomatic challenges before us, at the changing region around us, and remember the issues tearing us apart from within, to understand that an immense responsibility rests upon us,” Herzog said.
Netanyahu remains prime minister in a caretaker government until a new coalition is formed or there is another election, which must be held if no candidate succeeds.
Though the 77-year-old political veteran did better than expected in the vote and his Likud party won the most seats, his nationalist-religious coalition, the most rightwing government in Israel’s history, lost its governing majority.

Donald Trump is a president without parallel, but history can still be instructive. Lame duck presidents often focus on foreign policy to escape domestic discontent and establish a legacy in an area where a hostile Congress offers less of an obstacle. Mr Trump, who was stunningly rebuffed by voters in Tuesday’s midterms, might seek satisfaction in construction projects, the 2028 presidential race and his family’s future. Or, amid the humiliation and with Republican critics growing louder, he could distract attention with fresh adventurism – perhaps escalating against Cuba – or more likely a vengeful new offensive against Iran.
Mr Trump won’t put in the legwork or attention to detail demanded by, say, Bill Clinton’s push for lasting peace in the Middle East. But he loves the glitz of state visits, spectacular military action, hobnobbing with strongmen and (unearned) credit for dubious “peace deals”. With a potential three-way meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping mooted for the Apec summit in China this month, Ukraine, Taiwan and others have reason to be nervous.
“The reason we lost [the midterms] is the war,” wrote JD Vance, the vice-president, on X. Mr Trump himself acknowledged Iran’s impact. Though voters don’t always connect action overseas to consequences at home, the link to higher prices was clear. Resuming the bombing would only deepen the crisis. The president has so far withstood Benjamin Netanyahu’s blandishments to renew their illegal war, and the Israeli prime minister is now fighting for political survival after last month’s election. But a negotiated exit looks more difficult than ever. A more militarised and hardline regime in Iran has seen the advantages of broadening the conflict and is crowing over Tuesday’s results.
Mr Trump has accelerated the expansion of executive authority over war, rejecting congressional constraint, and now says he will be “Mr Veto” if the legislature proves a problem. But Democrats’ seizure of Congress, which controls government spending, nonetheless gives them significant new power. They can increase pressure by tying their goals to “must-pass” legislation, though threatening a government shutdown over foreign policy comes with political risks. Control of appropriations committees will enable closer scrutiny of what is being spent, and where. Anti-interventionist Republicans will be reinvigorated – though the president vetoed a bipartisan resolution to end support for Saudi Arabia’s war in Yemen in his first term.
At a minimum, the Democrats can increase transparency and accountability for this administration’s crimes and follies, including its treatment of Ukraine and attacks on alleged drugs boats. Investigating the Trump circle’s links with foreign powers and business people could prove especially powerful: voters are increasingly concerned about corruption now that critics have tied it to the affordability crisis.
The midterms are an unusually powerful reminder that foreign and domestic policy cannot be sundered and that voters as well as the leaders they pick shape a country’s relationship with the world. Mr Vance was also striking in stressing the need to “change our relationship to Israel”. Like Mr Trump’s abrupt claim that the US would end military aid by the end of the year, that is a belated response to a seismic shift in public opinion – with most Americans now holding unfavourable views of their ally thanks to Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza, and Mr Netanyahu’s pursuit of permawar in the region.
American voters, and people around the world, must hope that newly elected Democrats will be deft in using their new levers to shape US actions. But when voters’ opinions are so strongly held and expressed, that moulds policy too.

Russia arranged to supply Iran with 90 launchers for advanced guided missiles, according to leaked defence industry documents that shed light on the depth of military cooperation between Moscow and Tehran.
The documents, obtained by Dallas Analytics, a Ukrainian private intelligence firm, and shared with the Guardian, detail plans to supply Iran with launchers for the LMUR, a guided missile fired from attack helicopters which Russian forces have used extensively against Ukrainian targets since the full-scale invasion in 2022.
A production schedule drawn up in May 2024 by Vympel, a leading Russian designer of missiles and launch systems, lists an order for 90 launchers under an export contract designated “K-10”, with deliveries scheduled between late 2024 and December 2025. Separate internal paperwork explicitly identifies K-10 as Iran.
The records do not establish whether the launchers were ultimately delivered. However, a separate production schedule listing six Yak-130 jet trainers destined for Iran in 2023 is consistent with publicly reported deliveries of the aircraft.
The files offer fresh insight into Russian-Iranian military cooperation at a sensitive moment as Washington weighs its next steps in its war against Iran after the US midterm elections.
Observers widely regard Moscow as one of the main winners of a prolonged war in Iran, which has brought Russia strategic and economic advantages.
Russia has benefited from an increase in global energy prices triggered by disruptions to shipping through the strait of Hormuz and attacks on energy infrastructure across the Gulf. Higher oil revenues give the Kremlin an additional source of funds for its war in Ukraine and could help ease pressure on Russia’s strained budget.
The war has also diverted international attention and western military resources away from Ukraine, further straining Kyiv’s access to crucial US-made Patriot air defence interceptors.
Donald Trump has repeatedly played down the extent of Moscow’s support for Iran. Last month, the US president wrote that Russia was doing “very little, if anything” to help Tehran, arguing that he did not want to drive Moscow away from negotiations to end the war in Ukraine.
Trump’s claims contrast with European intelligence findings that Russia has provided Iran with key data and satellite images that could help it target US forces in the Middle East.
European intelligence agencies have also warned that Moscow was preparing to supply Tehran with explosive-laden drones for use against the US and Israel.
Military cooperation between Russia and Iran has expanded significantly since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, when Tehran became a crucial supplier of Shahed attack drones, which Russia has since begun manufacturing domestically.
Moscow has denied reports that it is supplying military equipment to Iran for use in the current conflict. The two countries signed a strategic partnership agreement in 2025 that includes provisions for countering shared threats, although it stops short of the mutual defence commitments contained in Russia’s security pact with North Korea.
But Tehran and Moscow have kept in very close cooperation in recent months.
In October alone, senior Russian and Iranian officials held three high-level meetings, underscoring the growing importance both governments attach to their relationship.
Moscow has been careful not to publicise its military cooperation with Tehran, wary of jeopardising Putin’s relationship with Trump. Russia also faces constraints on its ability to supply Iran with weapons, with much of its military production already stretched by the demands of the war in Ukraine.
The leaked documents provide a glimpse into the pressures facing Russia’s defence industry. In the May 2024 letter, Vympel warned that delays in the supply of essential components threatened the assembly of missile launchers and risked disrupting Russian state defence contracts.

La respuesta corta es que los norteamericanos dieron un vuelco total a la política en Estados Unidos, esmerilando o acabando con diez años de nacionalismo autoritario de Donald Trump al arrebatarle el control del Legislativo. Algo parecido ha sucedido días antes en Israel, con el polémico gobierno de Benjamín Netanyahu, también privado de sus mayorías parlamentarias, claves en la íntima sociedad que construyó con su aliado norteamericano. Un ciclo de novedades que tuvo en la victoria de Lula da Silva en Brasil el golpe más severo a la arquitectura dominante que el canciller Marco Rubio edificó para Trump en esta región y que suma ahora el mal trago de Paraguay.
La respuesta larga busca el hilo que une a esos episodios y a otros que conmocionan en estas horas a naciones del centro europeo o de su periferia en Albania, y más allá hasta en Asia. Un cambio de ciclo que se explica en el colapso del contrato que debería garantizar que el sistema contenga y realice. Como eso no sucede, hay un regreso de los indignados, el movimiento que, como señalaba el sociólogo Ulrich Beck, se eleva desde la calle a las instituciones en demanda de una mejora de ese sistema. El movimiento “cucarachas” de la India tiene esa impronta.
Los indignados nacieron después del gran tsunami económico y financiero de 2008 y carecían de dirigentes; simplemente sucedía. La comparación es provocadora si se la acerca al capítulo que acaba de vivir EE.UU. Allí, al menos en la superficie, queda claro que quien ha perdido, y de manera definitiva, es el presidente Donald Trump. Pero del otro lado no hay un líder que confronte, sino un enorme puñado de dirigencias demócratas y algunos republicanos alejados de la línea tóxica de la variante MAGA. Un dato nítido del comicio, es que se votó primero contra Trump y luego, posiblemente, por las propuestas de la oposición.
No se debe exagerar, sin embargo, con la noción de que esto fue solo producto de una irritación lógica de masas exhaustas por el implacable autoritarismo nacionalista del gobierno y sus derivas reaccionarias. Hay, en cambio, un amplio sector del establishment que habría decidido el relevo de un dirigente que, con la guerra en Irán, su repudio al libre mercado con ofensivas arancelarias proteccionistas y la cacería de inmigrantes, puso en riesgo el lugar de poder y de acumulación de la principal potencia capitalista. También, por un aislacionismo que deja a Europa en la distancia al igual que a China, coquetea con Rusia y concentra la atención en apenas América Latina.
Con el hartazgo popular apareció un resquicio para ese relevo. Es lo que algunos analistas llaman el “tiempo de la venganza” con el regreso del liberalismo y el inicio del peor momento para Trump si es que logra gobernar los próximos dos años, cuestión que merece desde ahora una considerable duda. Pocas horas después de las elecciones, Hakeem Jeffries, señalado como el próximo titular de la Cámara de Diputados bajo control demócrata, advirtió que el Congreso “pondrá freno a un Poder Ejecutivo fuera de control”. Para que quede claro hasta dónde están dispuestos a llegar, Jeffries aludió a lo que llamó el “Cártel Trump de corrupción masiva... Haremos que los delincuentes rindan cuentas”.
El distanciamiento, casi inmediato, del vicepresidente JD Vance, es una señal a tono con lo que se viene. Nada que asombre. Vale recodar que este funcionario en un mensaje en 2016 escribía lo siguiente: “Dudo entre pensar que Trump es un imbécil cínico como Nixon, que no sería tan malo, o que es el Hitler de América”. La referencia a Nixon hoy puede ser especialmente antipática para Trump por lo que evoca. Aquel presidente renunció para evitar su impeachment.
Como evalúan politólogos y constitucionalistas estadounidenses (David Golove de la Universidad de Nueva York, o juristas del Brennan Center for Justice) es poco probable que Trump se retire voluntariamente o acepte un rol pasivo, pero la pérdida de mayorías legislativas lo deja acorralado.
